content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

A little over twenty years ago I saw a production of “Endgame” at the Matrix Theatre in L.A.  It was directed by Andrew Robinson and the cast I saw (they rotated) featured Robin Gammell as Hamm, Allan Arbus as Nagg, Claudette Sutherland as Nell and Cotter Smith as Clov.

I don’t know why or how it happened, but that production was the first time I felt keyed in to Beckett.  It seemed that this production revealed Beckett’s intention – to examine time.  To pull it apart the way a scientist pulls apart an insect under a microscope.  Robinson’s direction was crystal clear and the performances were without embellishment, leaving the characters and the story free to wander through our minds.

What I learned from that 1995 production still holds, and this production of “Endgame” is a welcome place to visit. No matter the bleak setting of the tale.  This “Endgame” is worth the trip  to the Irish Arts Center located on the far reaches of the West Side. The very far reaches.

This production of Endgame comes to us from Galway’s Druid, a touring theater company that was founded 50 years ago.  Garry Hynes, this production’s director, was one of the founding members.  An interview with her and one of the other co-founders, Marie Mullen, can be found here.

“Endgame” is an investigation into an ending that is promised but never arrives.  Despite the protestations of Hamm (Rory Nolan) who is central to the staging as well as the story.  The endgame is upon us (in case you had forgotten) but the end is still elusive.  In the mean time we are invited to watch the few people left on earth while away the minutes that are never ending, until they amount to something that is an ending.

Grain upon grain, one by one, and one day, suddenly, there’s a heap, a little heap, the impossible heap.

Watching gains of time accumulate is not as boring as it may sound.  Each moment is a small combustible engine that fires off every few seconds as if Beckett is testing to see if we are paying attention.  Hamm is a decaying leftover of a man who now has only his manservant Clov (Aaron Monaghan) whose main job is to remind Hamm that life IS happening.

ENDGAME: Aaron Monaghan and Rory Nolan; Photo by HanJie Chow

The two are paired by disabilities.  Hamm cannot walk and Clove cannot sit.  Hamm cannot see what is on the other side of the elevated dungeon windows (kudos to Francis O’Connor and James F. Ingalls for set and lighting design respectively) that transform into the eyes of the world as we watch.  Clov can and chooses to look out the windows at Hamm’s command and narrates the slow demise of the world he sees.

In addition to this pair are Hamm’s parents, Mother (Marie Mullen) and Father (Bosco Hogan) neatly contained in two trash-bins.  These two only appear when called, and their presence gives us the proof that Hamm was once more than what he is presently.  The storage place for the parents seems logical – who hasn’t considered the same idea?  Anyone?

ENDGAME: Bosco Hogan and Marie Mullen; HanJie Chow

This foursome plays a slow but intriguing game of something-or-other.  Lines are tossed, caught and returned.  Each syllable, each motion, each subtle change of light in this dungeon are handed out judiciously because each is a full blown sphere holding a universe.  The words connect like a chain link fence. Little by little, this most excellent ensemble delivers up the grains of the tale without hesitating or letting any single one drop until, voilà – we come round to the place where we began.

Life is not linear.  It is circular.  Watch  your back.

ENDGAME by Samuel Beckett’s Endgame, directed by Garry Hynes

WITH Aaron Monaghan as Clov, Rory Nolan as Hamm, Marie Mullen as Nell, and Bosco Hogan as Nagg.

The creative team includes Francis O’Connor (Set and Costume Designer), James F. Ingalls(Lighting Designer), Gregory Clarke(Sound Designer), Gráinne Coughlan(Hair and Make-Up Designer), and Clíodhna Hallissey (Associate Costume Designer

Through November 23 at the Irish Arts Center, 726 11th Ave at 51st Street.  TICKETS HERE.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: American Lyric Theater’s Luminous Anniversary Gala

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Tonight was a celebration of  20 years of vision, artistry, and the transformative power of new opera.

With inspired comments and introductions from ALT founder Lawrence Edelson, Thursday evening at Merkin Hall offered more than just a concert—it delivered a revelation. American Lyric Theater‘s twentieth anniversary gala demonstrated with unmistakable clarity why sustained artistic mentorship matters, why the patient cultivation of creative partnerships yields extraordinary fruit, and why the future of American opera burns so brightly. The atmosphere crackled with anticipation as audience members gathered to witness not merely performances but a living testament to two decades of transformative work in the operatic arts.

L-R: Susan Feder. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR, Royce Vavrek, Librettist. Courtesy roycevaverek.com, Lawrence Edelson. Founder, Artistic Director, and General Director of American Lyric Theater. Courtesy altnyc.org

One thinks of Leonard Bernstein‘s celebrated observation that “music can name the unnameable and communicate the unknowable”—and indeed, throughout this evening’s extraordinary showcase of contemporary American opera, we witnessed precisely such feats of artistic alchemy, as the fruits of ALT’s pioneering Composer Librettist Development Program demonstrated the profound depths to which collaboration between words and music can illuminate the human condition.

The Visionary Foundation: Honoring Susan Feder

The evening featured a well-deserved tribute to Susan Feder, whose fifteen-year tenure as a program officer at the Mellon Foundation proved instrumental—one might say indispensable—to ALT’s evolution from a modest startup into a premier cultural incubator. Feder spoke with characteristic elegance about the newly established fellowship bearing her name, her words suffused with the rare wisdom she had gleaned over decades of nurturing artistic excellence. Moreover, her presence reminded us that great operas, as ALT’s tagline rightfully proclaims, genuinely don’t just happen—they require visionaries who understand that the future of opera depends not merely on commissions and productions, but on the sustained development of the artists who create them.

L-R: Jonathan Michie, Baritone. Karen Vuong, Soprano, Justin Hopkins, Bass Baritone. Courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

Cultivating Tomorrow’s Masterworks: The CLDP Legacy

At the heart of this celebration stood the remarkable legacy of the Composer Librettist Development Program (CDL),  America’s only full-time professional mentorship initiative for operatic writers. Furthermore, the evening’s centerpiece revelation—a preview of “Dear Little Chap” from Missy Mazzoli and Royce Vavrek‘s Lincoln in the Bardo—served as a luminous testament to the program’s efficacy.

Varek was on hand to speak about the commission by The Metropolitan Opera for its anticipated 2026 world premiere of Lincoln in the Bardo. The Met’s upcoming performance of this work represents a watershed moment: the first opera by a CLDP alumna to grace the hallowed stage of America’s premier opera house. Vavrek spoke eloquently of his formative years in the program, his remarks illuminating the profound impact of ALT’s unique pedagogical approach—one that treats librettists and composers as equal collaborators in the sacred act of operatic creation.

A Tapestry of American Voices

The evening’s program traversed an impressive panorama of contemporary operatic achievement, each excerpt offering its own distinctive contribution to the evolving canon of American opera.

From Jeremy Howard Beck and Stephanie Fleischmann‘s emotionally searing The Long Walk—based on Brian Castner‘s haunting memoir—to Derrick Wang‘s witty Scalia/Ginsburg and Jasmine Arielle Barnes and Deborah D.E.E.P. Mouton‘s She Who Dared, the selections revealed the remarkable breadth of ALT’s artistic vision.

Works like Christopher Cerrone and Tony Asaro‘s All Wounds Bleed and Aleksandra Vrebalov and Deborah Brevoort‘s The Knock demonstrated how contemporary opera can engage with urgent social and political questions.

At the same time, Ricky Ian Gordon and Royce Vavrek‘s The House Without A Christmas Tree and Alex Weiser and Stephanie Fleischmann‘s Tevye’s Daughters explored the timeless territories of family, memory, and belonging.

L-R: Andrew Bidlack, Tenor, Caroline Worra, Soprano. Ethan Vincent. Baritone. Photos courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

The assembled artists brought these diverse works to vivid life with consistently impressive artistry. Baritones Jonathan Michie and Gideon Dabi navigated complex emotional terrain with remarkable nuance, while mezzo-sopranos Heather Johnson and Gina Perregrino brought depth and color to their respective roles. Tenor Andrew Bidlack‘s clarion sound and bass-baritone Justin Hopkins’ commanding presence added further luster to the proceedings. Soprano Karen Vuong demonstrated exceptional versatility across multiple selections, while Jacqueline Echols McCarley’s dramatic intensity proved particularly striking in excerpts from She Who Dared. Soprano Jennifer Zetlan distinguished herself with coloratura passages of crystalline precision and an interpretive depth that brought particular warmth to both the virtuosic demands of Scalia/Ginsburg and the poignant lyricism of Tevye’s Daughters. Soprano Caroline Worra and baritone Ethan Vincent rounded out this stellar ensemble with performances of consummate professionalism.

The Collaborative Spirit: Musical Leadership and Artistic Excellence

The evening’s pianists—Djordje Nesic, Kelly Kuo, and Jason Wirth—deserved special commendation for their sensitive and virtuosic accompaniments. These accomplished musicians served not merely as accompanists but as true collaborative partners, their playing revealing the intricate musical architecture of each work while supporting the vocalists with unwavering sensitivity. Their contribution exemplified the collaborative ethos that has defined ALT’s approach from its inception—the recognition that grand opera emerges not from individual genius alone, but from the confluence of many artistic streams flowing toward a shared vision.

Artistic Faith and Vision

Opera has always been the most complete of artistic expressions—a convergence of music, drama, visual spectacle, choreography, and narrative that creates something greater than the sum of its parts. In the nineteenth century, audiences entered opera houses seeking precisely this kind of total immersion, an opportunity to suspend disbelief and inhabit worlds both fantastical and profoundly human. Each listener brought their own understanding to the unfolding story, making the experience simultaneously collective and deeply personal. Today, while technological innovations offer new possibilities for spectacle and scenic transformation, opera’s essential power remains rooted in something far more elemental: the dedicated artistry of singers, instrumentalists, dancers, visual artists, and creators who devote their lives to mastering this demanding craft. It is this human dimension—the voice that can convey joy and anguish in a single phrase, the composer who labors to capture an ineffable emotion in notation, the librettist who finds the precise words to unlock meaning—that continues to make opera uniquely capable of piercing through our contemporary distractions to touch something essential in the human spirit.

Gideon Babi, Baritone. Courtesy gideonbabi.com. Jennifer Zetlan, Soprano. Courtesy jenniferzetlan.com

As the evening drew to its post-champagne-toasted denouement, one reflected on the profound significance of what Lawrence Edelson and his colleagues have achieved over these two decades. Like the great impresarios of opera’s golden age—yet working within distinctly contemporary circumstances—ALT has created an institution that nurtures productions and artists, not spectacles but sustainable artistic collaborations. The result is a body of work that has already begun to enrich the operatic repertoire, with ALT alums’s compositions performed by more than 125 companies worldwide.

In this age when so much of our cultural discourse centers on preservation and nostalgia, American Lyric Theater reminds us that the operatic tradition remains vital precisely because it continues to evolve, to embrace new voices and new stories, to find fresh ways of articulating those essential human truths that transcend any single era or aesthetic. As we departed into the October evening, the melodies and words of this remarkable program still resonating in our consciousness, we carried with us not merely memories of beautiful performances but renewed faith in opera’s capacity to surprise, to challenge, and to illuminate the depths of human experience.

L-R Jacqueline Echols, Soprano. Heather Johnson, Mezzo Soprano. Gina Perregrino, Mezzo Soprano. Photos courtesy Michelle Tabnick PR

content.rendered:
By David Walters

 

“When you are not fed love on a silver spoon, you learn to lick it off of knives.” – poet Lauren Eden

Everyone has their own idea of what love is. Their love language. What makes them feel seen, heard, and safe.

Ones’ love language is expressed in many different ways, from the kind that wraps you like a warm blanket right out of the dryer, to the kind that inflicts physical and psychological harm in order to toughen up a person for the cruel world. All given and inflicted out of “love.”

Zoë Kim grew up with the latter. Her journey that brought her to The Public’s Shiva Theater stage has been her searching for the former. What she shares with the audience is her revolution, her journey, her voyage into self and what she needs as an adult that she didn’t get as a child.

It is so very difficult to change who we are, to morph into someone else beyond what our parents and our upbringing have endowed us with, to change and learn how to love ourselves. Psychologists and meditation gurus purport that is our only true goal in life. Zoë does that every night of this production. By sharing her journey and you witnessing it, there may be hope for us all.

The title, DID YOU EAT? (밥 먹었니?), comes from suppressed meanings of Zoë’s mother’s inability to say what she was truly feeling. Instead of, “I’m worried about you,” “I’m sorry,” or “How are you?” she would use a rendition of, “Did you eat?” to express that feeling.

We often give to others from our love language even though the person we’re giving to doesn’t speak our dialect, much less our language of love. If we don’t take the time to figure out what language the other person speaks, we may never be able to communicate in any worthwhile way. Misunderstandings all around.

I really can’t say that this is a Korean/American story and what struck me in my heart is that it is a human story first. What Zoe experienced in her life translates to anywhere on this earth where we humans tred. The autobiographical journey that Zoë takes her audience on is as much a dance as it is a telling. Zoë’s graceful movements, with intricate choreography by Iris McCloughan, creates a unique presentation that allows some of the pressure of childhood trauma to escape and gives the audience a chance to breathe. The projections by Yee Eun Nam and lighting by Minjoo Kim act as music accompaniment to the piece adding to the tensions and highlighting the different moods and movements as the play progresses.

What you come out with after the show is over is the personal strength of Zoë Kim. Her life could have broken a person with lesser conviction and as she plunges down the rabbit hole of her life’s journey and a respect for human endurance. Zoe’s journey to love through her life is pretty horrific. She has come to a place of self-respect and growth that was absent from the beginning. this presentation is cathartic for her, and brave, and riveting, and hopefully reflects back on you and the choices you’ve made in your life, surrounding what love is to you and those close to you.

Love each other.

—–
DID YOU EAT? (밥 먹었니?) was written and performed by Zoë Kim. Directed by Chris Yejin. Choreographed by Iris McCloughan.

Scenic design by Tanya Orellana, costume design by Harriet Jung, lighting design by Minjoo Kim, sound design by Tae Jong Park, projection design by Yee Eun Nam, dramaturgy by Amrita Ramanan,

Tickets can be accessed by visiting publictheater.org, calling 212.967.7555, or in person at the Taub Box Office at The Public Theater at 425 Lafayette Street through Sunday, November 16.
Running time is 70 minutes with no intermission
Triggers: the play addresses complex and sensitive topics including experiences of childhood trauma, self-harm, and suicidal ideation.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Now through November 2 at Soho Playhouse, the solo comedy show Unstuck  is entertaining audiences with a mashup of the manifestations of OCD and the self-discovery of being queer. This being akin to riding Steel Vengeance at Cedar Point (world’s wildest roller coaster), upside down. Expect things to come out of all orifices.

OCD, though often misunderstood, is a chronic mental health condition that can become all-encompassing and take over someone’s life to the extent that they see themselves and everyone around them only through this lens. It focuses on the things that the person cares most about, and laser beams a false sense of power over them.

Olivia Levine tells her raw and honest story of growing up, finding out who she is, and learning to become unstuck in her life. This wild ride through her life is both entertaining and horrifying at the same time.in her sharing that brings about an understanding and a comradery. Is it the constant laughs? Is it her disarmingly inviting smile?

I used the word raw earlier because in Unstuck she shares the true depths of her OCD, how it manifests itself, and how she has figured out how to move in this world saddled with the compulsions that overtake her. In revealing herself, she, metaphorically, not only takes off her clothes for us to see the real her, but sheds her skin, reaches deeper inside and cracks her ribs open so we can see the guts of who she is. Cringy sometimes, yes. But much more than brave on her part revealing her most private moments in such an open way. What makes it work and keeps us from turning away and keeps this show from being a traumalogue, is her personal charm and her great gift to be able to laugh at herself, causing the audience to laugh along with her. A priceless gift. She has an open and inviting personality that makes you want to keep your eyes wide-open as she strips herself of all the veneer that we humans usually shelter ourselves with.

Revealing her awareness of her sexuality and how that did and did not translate to having a relationship, her obsession with masturbation, her fixation on preventing her parents from dying, she invites us to share in her self-realization. She does this symbolically at the top of the show by sharing her orange(s) with the audience. A nice way to build immediate rapport. To keep it throughout the show, she’s just herself, her complete self, and the audience loves her for it.

—–

Unstuck, written and performed by Olivia Levine and directed by Molly Rose Heller.

Tickets can be purchased HERE.

The show has a running time of 60 minutes and is recommended for 18+ audiences.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Every season there’s one or two shows that are just too painful to sit through.

Unfortunately, Art of Leaving is one of those.

And I’m not saying the performance itself was of poor quality; the cast was fine. Rather, it was the show’s presentation of masculinity–

Art of Leaving, written by Anne Marilyn Lucas and directed by Matt Gehring, examines what a marriage can be through different generations and the decisions that will literally break or continue the relationship. Though in either situation, there seems to be at least one person disappointed. The piece opens in an extremely clean, organized, and gray apartment where Aaron (Jordan Lage) and Diana (Audrey Heffernan Meyer) reside together. It actually reminds me of the set for a sit-com. Aaron’s flexing in front of a mirror, lecturing his wife on how to properly prepare his health smoothies, and rebuking her decision to buy him turkey instead of chicken. Is this a midlife crisis or honestly a huge flaw of Aaron? Because I sense that he’s always been this insecure, self-centered, finicky man.

I wonder if Aaron and Diana are a new couple, a one-night stand, or newly married. I would not have guessed they were about to celebrate their twentieth-fifth wedding anniversary, but, maybe this is intentional.

Aaron is obsessed with a men’s self-help guru who seemingly does not support anything that could potentialy diminish an ounce of a man’s masculinity. Aaron treats this man as a prophet, his book Male Satisfaction Over 40 as a gift from above, and fully subscribes to him to a very, very unhealthy level. While this is clear to the audience, I expected this to become a hot topic in Aaron and Diana’s marriage, but instead the guru’s teachings became motivation for Aaron decide whether this marriage was really satisfying him. 

While Diana continues through her day at work, I feel a bit of sympathy for her but disgusted that she has allowed this man who physically pounds self-affirmations into his chest in front of a mirror to be such a commanding figure in her life. The contrast of this 50-year old man ridiculously controlling his wife with their son (Brian Mason) and his fiancé (Molly Chiffer) is laughable but also realistic in this day and age. This young couple in their 20’s are navigating a relationship that’s one-sided in a desire for a poly-amorous marriage. Cue the addition of Aaron’s parents, Esther (Pamela Shaw) and Felix (Alan Ceppos) to the living room, and we have a whole family who are unsatisfied in their relationships but think they know what is best for Aaron and Diana.

The old-school stereotypes that fly out of Esther’s mouth make the audience groan, and it’s a bit much that I’m also shifting in my seat, uncomfortable. Whether the middle-aged and older singles and married couples in the audience surrounding me connected to this or not, the dialogue was a lot. An embarrassing level of masculine stereotyping takes over Aaron and the appropriateness that Esther and Diana find in their husbands hurt.

These three generations come together, in Aaron’s living room, when Aaron drops a bombshell on his wife, Diana. We wonder if Diana will be strong enough to make a decision that prioritizes her own self-satisfaction and happiness, or if the couple will work out their gripes with identity and self-worth in this seemingly love-less marriage.

Ultimately, every stereotype of aging men, midlife crises, and couple conflicts are referenced on stage. It was like there was a checklist of clichés, stereotypical lines to say that would make the audience hate men and the relationship dynamics of those in their 20’s and those in their 50’s alike.

I would give this one big cringe.

Written by Anne Marilyn Lucas; directed by Matt Gehring.

STARRING: Audrey Heffernan Meyer (Diana), Jordan Lage (Aaron), Alan Ceppos (Felix), Pamela Shaw (Esther), Molly Chiffer (Caitlyn), and Brian Mason (Jason).

CREATIVE TEAM: Dan Hasse (Dramaturg), Frank Oliva (Scenic Designer), Lara De Bruijn (Costume Designer), Kevin Foster (Wig Designer), Betsy Chester (Lighting Designer), and Ben Vigus (Sound Designer).

Art of Leaving is playing Off-Broadway at The Alice Griffin Jewel Box Theatre, The Pershing Square Signature Center, 480 West 42nd Street,  New York. Art of Leaving is not a Signature production.

Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

You only have a few more opportunities to see “Adam Gopnik’s New York”, (it closes on the 26th) billed as a “theatrical event” which is an honest appraisal.  This is not a one-person show as we think of them.  A one-person show implies that the person on the stage is an actor.  Gopnik is not an actor.  He is an extraordinary writer and observer who has found in his home town plenty to observe.

Gopnik is a jewel of a writer. He drifts from subject to subject  as if he were reading from a book of his own essays.  Within each story there is a beginning, middle and end.  He goes deep where most of us would pass by the subject on our way to one thing or another.

Did you know that Olmsted designed Central Park as a social project?  Its purpose was the coming together of people for the “practice of pleasure” – which was an extraordinary idea wrapped up in nature.  Politics, social standing, money or the lack thereof would divide us, but in Central Park our common shared goal was pleasure.  Gopnik tells us the park is his political philosophy.

There is the story of the story of “Proust and the Sex Rats” – no more needed there.

He explains his article “Quattrocento Baseball” that attempted to work out his profession as an art critic and student of fifteenth-century Italian art and also being fan of the Montreal Expos.

Did you know that snowflakes start out their lives as identical entities?  It is only through their journey to earth that they are reshaped into the individual objects they become.  Huh.  Kind of like life wouldn’t you say?

Snowflakes? Not something most of us talked about until Gopnik put it in our sight lines.

Joseph Mitchell, who had been at the New Yorker nearly 50 years by the time Gopnik arrived in 1986, said that the best writers had a “wild exactitude” in their work.  This phrase became a benchmark for Gopnik.  His writing mightily succeeds and this event comes close to Mitchell’s ideal.

And that is how the event rolls out.  One essay after another strung together by the teller.  There is no director listed, and that is the one thing this writer would suggest.  Gopnik puts enormous pressure on himself by memorizing 90 minutes worth of thoughtful writing.  It would be just as compelling if he read it.  As it is, his pauses are often distracting and lack specificity.  I wondered more than once if he had forgotten his line or could not decide what story would be next.

As he tells us from the beginning – he is not something you can move past by swiping.  He is a three dimensional being – as are we all.  Next time out (and I hope there is one) I hope he gets the stage guidance that his writing deserves.

Adam Gopnik’s New York Producers: Steve Martin and James L. Nederlander

The autobiographical solo show will play October 17-26 at The Clark Studio Theater at Lincoln Center (Samuel B. & David Rose Building, 165 West 65th Street).  Tickets are now on sale HERE.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: SurRound III: An Everlasting Journey of Hope

content.rendered:
By Ed Kliszus

In this halcyon evening, as we gathered within the transcendent embrace of the Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine, one could not help but feel the luminosity of something greater stirring—a celestial convergence of stone, spirit, and song. Indeed, when Musica Sacra presents its “SurRound” series under the sagacious direction of Maestro Kent Tritle, the experience transcends mere performance; it becomes, as Virginia Woolf might have whispered, a shimmering moment where time itself seems to pause and genuflect before beauty.

Hope as the Central Theme

Moreover, the very conception of this evening’s program—entitled “Everlasting Hope”—proved exquisitely prescient. As Maestro Tritle’s program notes eloquently revealed, a cease-fire in Gaza was announced the very morning rehearsals commenced for Thomas Tallis’s monumental Spem in Alium. The Latin word “Spem,” meaning hope, thus became not merely a title but a benediction, radiating through every subsequent selection with ineffable poignancy. Consequently, this theme of hope—from exaltation through lamentation to ultimate resolution—formed the eschatological architecture of an evening that would prove both burnin’ in its emotional intensity and crystalline in its technical execution.

The Cathedral’s Magnificent Acoustics and Immersive Design

The Cathedral’s magnificent acoustics, with their legendary five-second delay, transformed the venue into a veritable instrument unto itself. The singers, positioned around the audience in a 360-degree surround, literally enveloped the audience in waves of sound that seemed to emanate from the stones themselves. Subsequently, one experienced not merely the act of listening but of being inhabited by music—a synesthesia of spatial and sonic dimensions that proved revelatory. This immersive design, pioneered by Maestro Tritle for this series, exemplifies what programmatic music achieves at its apex: the marriage of architectural space with sonic expression.

The magnificent interior of the Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Opening Movements: From Gregorian Chant to Renaissance Splendor

Nevertheless, it was the superlative artistry of the vocalists that elevated the evening from the merely spectacular to the sublime. The program opened with the Gregorian chant Gloria in Excelsis, sung with such pellucid purity that five centuries seemed to evaporate in an instant. Undoubtedly, the ensemble’s impeccable diction, blend, and phrasing established immediately that we were in the presence of consummate professionals. As the opening strains floated upward into the Gothic vaulting, one felt the inaugural stirrings of hope—bright, confident, affirming.

Featured Soloists: Technical Mastery and Emotional Depth

Thereupon, Tallis’s Mass for Double Choir unfolded with ravishing beauty, the Kyrie sung with an elegiac quality that evoked medieval mystery. The phenomenal soloists—soprano Zen Wu, mezzo-soprano Hai-Ting Chinn, and tenor Gregorio Taniguchi—each brought distinctive coloratura to their contributions, their voices blending with stentorian power yet delicate refinement. Subsequently, Ralph Vaughan Williams’s meditative setting provided the perfect foil, its restrained Englishness offering a moment of introspection before the journey continued.

Sacred and Spiritual: A Dialogue Across Cultures

In addition, the juxtaposition of Arvo Pärt’s Da Pacem Domine with the traditional spiritual “Wade in the Water” proved particularly inspired. The former, with its characteristic tintinnabulation, floated ethereally through the space, while the latter—that quintessential American hymn of liberation—brought an earthy, visceral energy that set souls afire. Baritone Nathaniel Sullivan distinguished himself here with impressive strength and eloquent phrasing, his voice resonating with the gravitas of generations seeking freedom. Indeed, this dialectic between the sacred and the spiritual, between European mysticism and American resilience, encapsulated the evening’s broader theme: hope manifests across cultures, centuries, and continents.

Martin’s Agnus Dei and the Light of Hope

Equally compelling was Frank Martin’s Agnus Dei from his ravishing Mass for Double Choir. Soprano Kathryn McCreary navigated the fanciful, florid passages with aplomb, her voice soaring with sheer melodic rapture even as the ostinato in the second choir evoked the cosmic turning of spheres. Furthermore, the chant Lux Aeterna introduced music of light and hope with such radiant beauty that one could almost see the effulgent beams piercing through the Cathedral’s rose window.

The Evening’s Apex: Forty Voices Proclaiming Paradise

Nevertheless, it was Alessandro Striggio’s Ecce Beatam Lucem that proved the evening’s apex—the point toward which all prior music had been ascending. This stupendous work for forty voices, possibly composed in friendly rivalry with Tallis’s later masterpiece, filled the Cathedral with organized blocks of glorious sound. Mezzo-soprano Hai-Ting Chinn delivered the central solo passages with both technical mastery and profound emotional depth, while soprano Linda Jones brought clarion beauty to her featured moments. The text—”Behold the blessed light, behold eternal goodness”—became manifest through forty voices proclaiming paradise itself. Moreover, the subsequent chant In Paradisum flowed as a natural extension, as though angels themselves were guiding us toward that blessed shore.

Members of Musica Sacra at the Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine. Courtesy musicasacrany.com

Nancy Wertsch’s Contemporary Masterwork

Additionally, composer and chorus member Nancy Wertsch’s Antiphon for God the Father, incorporating texts by the illustrious Hildegard von Bingen, offered yet another spatial marvel. With the soloist positioned in the high pulpit and three choirs arrayed throughout the Cathedral, the music achieved a vertiginous three-dimensionality. This piece, dedicated to the memory of beloved organist Jim Christensen, carried particular poignancy—a testament to how music perpetuates memory and transforms grief into transcendent beauty.

Joseph Beutel’s Extraordinary Spiritual Performance

Likewise, the traditional African American spirituals brought the concert full circle, returning to hope’s most immediate and human expression. However, it was bass-baritone Joseph Beutel’s splendid, stentorian performance of “We’ll Understand It Better By and By” that emerged as one of the evening’s most profoundly moving moments. His deep, resonant voice—possessing both commanding power and tender vulnerability—captured the spiritual’s essential message with breathtaking eloquence. Furthermore, Beutel navigated the emotional terrain with such assurance that every phrase seemed to contain both the weight of suffering and the promise of eventual understanding. His interpretation transcended mere technical excellence; it became, instead, a sermon in song, a testament to faith’s sustaining power through tribulation. Indeed, as his voice filled the Cathedral’s vastness, one sensed generations of voices joining his—those who had sung this hymn through slavery’s darkness, through Jim Crow’s indignities, through every trial that tests the human spirit. Consequently, when Beutel reached the refrain, the audience sat transfixed, many visibly moved to tears by the sheer authenticity and depth of his artistry.

Moses Hogan’s Exuberant Arrangement

Subsequently, Moses Hogan’s thrilling arrangement of “I’m Gonna Sing ‘Til the Spirit Moves in My Heart” provided an exuberant contrast, its rhythmic vitality and call-and-response structure setting the entire Cathedral pulsing with joyous energy. Mezzo-soprano Tracy Cowart brought both scholarly precision and heartfelt warmth to her featured passages. Furthermore, Caroline Shaw’s tender setting of Psalm 84, “and the swallow,” provided an intimate interlude, its delicate beauty a reminder that hope often whispers rather than shouts.

The Grand Finale: Tallis’s Spem in Alium

Ultimately, however, it was the return to Tallis—his monumental Spem in Alium, both in Kent Tritle’s restored Latin version and in its rare English variant “Sing and Glorify”—that bookended the evening with breathtaking symmetry. The forty voices, distributed throughout the Cathedral in eight choirs of five, created an acoustic phenomenon unlike any other. As the music passed from section to section, building toward those spectacular culminating moments, one experienced sonic rapture. The final notes seemed indeed to ring to eternity, their reverberations continuing long after the last breath was released.

Maestro Kent Tritle’s Masterful Leadership

Maestro Tritle’s superbly subtle and effective conducting complemented his illuminating program notes, which prepared audiences to delve fully into each musical selection. His gestures—economical yet eloquent—drew from the chorus singing of astonishing refinement: impeccable pitch, articulation, dynamics, and phrasing executed with both technical mastery and profound musicality. Indeed, the superlative program book, with its sagacious commentary and splendid translations, ensured exceptional accessibility for all listeners, democratizing what might otherwise seem recondite knowledge.

Maestro Kent Tritle. Photo by Jennifer Taylor

A Luminous Evening of Hope and Beauty

To conclude, this “SurRound III” concert embodied everything that makes Musica Sacra’s artistry nonpareil: intellectual rigor married to emotional authenticity, historical scholarship wedded to living interpretation, and technical excellence serving ultimately the most human of expressions—hope. As we departed into the cool October evening, one carried within that hope like a flame carefully cupped against the wind. Moreover, knowing that Musica Sacra’s 2025-26 season promises further such revelations, one can only echo the sentiment of the spirituals: we will understand it better by and by, but for now, we are blessed simply to have experienced this foretaste of paradise. For those seeking to explore more about symphonic and choral music traditions, this performance stands as a luminous exemplar of the form at its most transcendent.

Experience Musica Sacra’s 2025-26 Season

Don’t miss Musica Sacra’s extraordinary upcoming season, featuring masterworks by Mozart and Handel, as well as world premieres. Under Maestro Tritle’s visionary direction, these concerts promise transcendent experiences that nourish the soul and elevate the spirit in profound ways.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Oratorio for Living Things is as much as an individual experience as it is composed for a group. Signature Theatre’s Resident Heather Christian has brought a complex yet humble and angelic space for us to simultaneously feel and lose ourselves in time. The libretto sings time before us: how we use our time, and how time will move after us–our “memory harvest.” Whether we spend “Eleven hours wondering if something that you’re doing is normal” or “forty two hours looking at a clock,”  our reckoning of time is fused for roughly 90 minutes on a fall evening in Hell’s Kitchen. Maybe, we’ll all remember this hour and a half for the rest of our time, coalescing where violence and safety live together.

While the focus of Christian’s piece was muddled, and I had trouble connecting these ideas of violence and time, I was able to appreciate the experience of being present.

Simply, an awareness that an oratorio is a musical composition incorporating choir, solosits, instrumentals, and narrative storytelling through song and script is all you need to take in this piece. And, if you aren’t familiar with an “oratorio” before entering this surreal space, you’ll quickly be absorbed into the sound.

Ashley Pérez Flanagan, Ben Moss. Photo by Ben Arons.

Signature’s Romulus Linney Courtyard Theatre has been completely reworked from the normal theater setups where audience sit in rows or surrounding the stage. Instead, we are the set. The performers circle an orbbed light that rises, illuminating their faces and highlighting the blue color scheme that evokes some flow of calm that I can’t seem to put into words. Immediately, I’m aware that this work will be felt deeply, inexplainably.

The audience members surrounding me are as much of the show as the performers. We’re all aware of each other’s presence. The various audience reactions to this production encapsulates how differently each of us approach and feel this. Someone across from me meditates; a man seated in the first row–a chair on the floor–comes in and out of rest, a man across from me is completely drawn in, bursting with laughter at every even slightly humorous or witty line. The time passes quickly; it feels as though we’re all in this enclosed space, both entrapped and floating.

Divya Maus, Fraser Campbell, Ashley Perez Flanagan. Photo by Ben Arons.

The intricacies of this production are what stood out the most: the eye contact of these performers, directed into the audience, are unmatched. They keep us alive, but almost in a trance. Intentional, specific costuming by Márion Talán de la Rosa crafts this production into the harmony and stillness that remains with us, leaving the space. I could not appreciate more the red stitching of the buttons, red shoes, necklaces, the hemming of a shirt. Sometimes the reflection of light, or the minimalness spread of light, cast golden hues. The choir as a whole and individually is special, enormormously talented and bursting with this energy that balanced every part of the score and libretto.

Barrie Lobo McLain. Photo by Ben Arons.

I’m made more aware of memory and time–

how I choose to spend my time, or how time chooses to spend me–

this libretto–part in Latin and part in English–is brilliant. The merging of spirutality with science: when it’s not making us sink back into our seats and drift, it’s making us think:

thirteen months fighting a cold
seven years cleaning the same room over and over
seventeen minutes fighting the urge to touch someone’s face
six minutes saying “remember this” to yourself

…thirty one days looking for an outlet
five days calming someone down
ten years calming yourself down
four and a half years knowing someone is lying to your face
and not saying anything.

Ángel Lozada. Photo by Ben Arons.

Written by Heather Christian. Directed by Lee Sunday Evans. Music Direction by Ben Moss.

FEATURING: Kirstyn Cae Ballard, Jonathan Christopher, Carla Duren, Ashley Pérez Flanagan, Brian Flores, Jonny-James Kajoba, Ángel Lozada, Divya Maus, Barrie Lobo McLain, Ben Moss, Onyie Nwachukwu, Dito van Reigersberg.

UNDERSTUDIES: Major Curda, Laura Darrell, Elisa Galindez, Jacob Ryan Smith.

MUSICIANS: Jules Biber (Cello), Fraser Campbell (Winds), Jane Cardona (Pianist), John Murchison (Bass), Odetta Hartman (Violin), Peter Wise (Percussion). Conducted by Jane Cardona and Ben Moss.

CREATIVE TEAM: Emily Shooltz (Artistic Director), Timothy J. McClimon (Eexecutive Director), Krit Robinson (Scenic, Original Artwork & Environmental Design), Márion Talán de la Rosa (Costume Design), Nick Kourtides (Lighting Design).

Oratorio for Living Things is playing at The Pershing Square Signature Center’s Romulus Linney Courtyard Theatre, 480 W. 42nd St, New York, NY. Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Vicki Weisfeld

An Old-Fashioned Family Murder, which premiered Friday night at George Street Playhouse, New Brunswick, N.J., is first-rate old-fashioned fun! This new comedy-mystery, written by Joe DiPietro and directed by Larry Raben, will be delighting audiences through November 2. It’s Tony Award-winner DiPietro’s eighth production at the Playhouse, and he and the theater clearly work beautifully together.

Though I’ve enjoyed two of DiPietro’s historical plays (The Other Mrs. Wilson and Conscience), this is the first of his comedies, and it isn’t without historical resonance too. It nicely echoes the whodunnit tropes and characters of the Golden Age of detective stories, starting with the secluded ritzy Claythorne mansion, isolated by a dramatic storm (lots of stage lightning and thunder), and brought to life by a stellar cast.

Set in 1943, the opening scenes give Arthur Whittington (played by Tony Carlin)—an insufferably pedantic and self-satisfied author of second-rate mysteries—the chance to rattle on. One of his pet themes is why a mere woman could never be a stellar detective. (Yes, you know from this point on that a woman will put him in his place).

Over the course of the evening, the two twenty-something Claythorne sisters, Dotty (Caitlin Kinnunen), who dresses like her own grandmother, and Clarice (Allison Scagliotti), the epitome of glamour, plus Clarice’s fiancé, Jasper Jamison (Michael Evan Williams), a pool boy at the country club, come to loathe the author. He plays a game of what if? that reveals all three have a motive to kill the ancient Claythorne patriarch, soundly sleeping upstairs: Dotty, because she’s treated like a servant, Clarice because Daddy objects to Jasper, and Jasper himself. When Whittington reveals he’s been invited there in order to witness a new will the old man has created—one that cuts one of the daughters out entirely—that really puts the cat among the pigeons.

Now appears the leader of Dotty’s mystery book club, Shirley Peck (Sally Struthers) who has distinctly different views about lady detectives. When everyone goes to bed, a murder does occur. Again you’ll recognize the tropes of classic detective fiction, but DiPietro’s script is full of laugh-out-loud lines that make them fresh again. Police detective Paul Peck (James Taylor Odom), Mrs. Peck’s son, arrives to investigate.

Under the not-so-steely gaze of the law, the players circle each other warily. The sisters’ claws come out; the laughs do too. The doting Mrs. Peck and her somewhat bumbling son play off each other perfectly, chemistry that may in part reflect Struthers and Odom’s past stage appearances together. Struthers’s performance of a woman struggling (and mostly failing) to keep a low profile, to let her son shine, is fascinating to watch. Her gestures and expressions, no matter how small, are exactly right.

Production credits to Robert Andrew Kovach (elegant scenic design), Molly Walz (costumes), José Santiago (lighting), Roger Stoddard (sound), and Roxanne De Luna (hair and wigs).

Tickets for An Old-Fashioned Family Murder are available here or by calling 732-246-7717.

title.rendered: Oil & Whiskey: A Country Music Meditation on Modern Romance

content.rendered:
The Chain Theatre is where Nashville meets Manhattan in a spirited musical comedy.

In the grand tradition of theatrical commentary upon the human condition, one finds oneself contemplating the peculiar phenomenon of contemporary romantic entanglements as presented in Dax Wiley and Kit Nolan’s Oil & Whiskey, a country-western musical romp that delivers considerable material for philosophical rumination. Like George Bernard Shaw’s own observations on the marriage question in his prefaces, this production tackles the modern malaise of extended singlehood with the kind of sardonic wit that recalls Seinfeld‘s dissection of urban relationship neuroses—though here set to the twang of steel strings and the clink of whiskey glasses.

The Prelude: Musical Portents in the Gathering Dark

As the audience settled into The Chain Theatre‘s intimate embrace on West 36th Street, the sound system offered its own subtle overture to the evening’s themes. Cassandra Coleman’s “Bite My Tongue” drifted through the space—that achingly contemporary meditation on restraint and the words we dare not speak—followed by Haim’s “Summer Girl,” with its wistful evocation of fleeting romance and nostalgic longing. These musical selections proved no arbitrary choices but rather a carefully curated preface to the evening’s central inquiry: What do we say? What do we hold back? And how do we navigate the treacherous territory between honesty and self-preservation?

Isabel Stewart as Zelda in Oil and Whiskey back stage at the Chain Theatre. Photo by Liz Guenther

The juxtaposition of Coleman’s indie-folk introspection and Haim’s shimmering pop sensibility established the production’s own aesthetic territory—somewhere between raw emotional confession and polished theatrical entertainment. Like the programmatic music of the Romantic era, where Berlioz and Liszt used instrumental sound to narrate specific stories, these pre-show selections functioned as emotional guideposts, preparing the audience for a narrative steeped in unspoken desires and the particular anguish of knowing exactly what one should say while being constitutionally unable to say it. One immediately recognized that this would be an evening concerned not merely with romance, but with the elaborate dance of advance and retreat that characterizes modern courtship—where “biting one’s tongue” becomes both a survival mechanism and a tragic flaw.

The Dramatis Personae: Young Hearts in an Old Dance

The premise is deceptively simple: Zelda and Teddy, former lovers separated by time and geography, reconvene in a Lower East Side watering hole for what promises to be either reconciliation or final rupture. Director Adam Jepsen has assembled a quartet of performers whose energetic commitment to the material transforms what might have been a mere romantic trifle into something approaching a genuine theatrical inquiry into the nature of attraction, regret, and the human capacity for self-deception.

Jater Webb as Teddy in Oil and Whiskey back stage at the Chain Theatre. Photo by Liz Guenther

Isabel Stewart as Zelda delivers a performance of considerable charm and emotional nuance, her vocal work navigating the score’s demands with the kind of technical assurance that suggests serious training (indeed, her recent graduation from UNCSA’s drama program is evident). Opposite her, Jater Webb embodies Teddy with a particular masculine insouciance that makes such characters simultaneously infuriating and irresistible. Webb’s dual role as both actor and guitarist—seamlessly integrating his instrumental work with the three-piece pit ensemble on stage—demonstrates a musicianship that serves the character’s Nashville aspirations while grounding the performance in genuine artistry.

The Sage and the Sentinel: Supporting Players of Distinction

The production’s secret weapons prove to be Tanner McIntyre as Bree, Zelda’s protective roommate, and Levi Penley as Ray, the bar’s proprietor and unofficial Greek chorus. McIntyre brings a knowing skepticism to her role that recalls the sharp-tongued confidantes of Restoration comedy, while Penley’s Ray emerges as a figure of almost Shakespearean proportion—part Falstaff, part Puck, wholly committed to comedic exuberance. His featured number, “A Lone Star Cowboy,” provided moments of pure theatrical delight, the kind of showstopping digression that, like the great programmatic compositions of the symphonic tradition, tells its own complete story while advancing the larger narrative.

Isabel Stewart as Zelda and Jater Webb as Teddy in a scene from Oil and Whiskey at the Chain Theatre. Photo by Liz Guenther

The Musical Architecture: Country Music as Emotional Cartography

Nolan’s score demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of country music’s narrative traditions, evoking everything from honky-tonk heartbreak to bluegrass jubilation. The opening number “Jealous” establishes the central conflict with admirable economy, while “Seein’ You’s Like Drinkin’ Whiskey” offered one of the evening’s most affecting sequences—a meditation on intoxication both literal and metaphorical that would not have been out of place in the Great American Songbook.

The three-piece band, anchored by the outstanding guitar work of Andrew Miramonti on electric guitar and piano, provided muscular yet sensitive accompaniment throughout. Makani Eliot’s drumming and Cody Rahn’s bass work created a rhythmic foundation that never overwhelmed the vocalists—a delicate balance often lost in intimate theatrical spaces. Miramonti’s instrumental interludes and lead guitar particularly shone, his virtuosity recalling the kind of sophisticated country-rock fusion that emerged from Nashville’s more adventurous studios in recent decades.

Isabel Stewart as Zelda in a scene from Oil & Whiskey at the Chain Theatre. Photo by Liz Guenther

Scenic Evocation and Sartorial Splendor

The production design evoked a peculiar intersection of country authenticity and urban irony—cowboy boots on a Manhattan stage being no small feat of atmospheric conjuring. One was reminded of those glorious moments in The Blues Brothers when Ray Charles transformed a mere music shop into a temple of soul, or of the way certain establishments can exist as portals between worlds. The Chain Theatre on West 36th Street, that exemplar of off-Broadway intimacy, proved the ideal venue for such alchemy. In this black-box configuration, the audience becomes complicit in the action, close enough to register every knowing glance and whispered aside—an immersion impossible in larger commercial houses where distance breeds detachment.

The Philosophical Core: Love in the Age of Deferral

What elevates Oil & Whiskey beyond mere romantic comedy is its engagement with a peculiarly contemporary phenomenon: the extended adolescence of modern courtship. Like Seinfeld’s characters perpetually circling commitment, Zelda and Teddy represent a generation for whom marriage and permanence remain perpetually deferred possibilities. Wiley’s book, while maintaining comic velocity, never condescends to its characters’ struggles. The recurring motif of failed reconciliation—examined through numbers like “The Fight” and the poignant “Oil & Water”—suggests that some incompatibilities transcend good intentions.

Jater Webb as Teddy in a scene from Oil and Whiskey at the Chain Theatre. Photo by Liz Guenther

There exists in Shaw’s dramatic criticism a persistent interest in what he termed “the life force”—that biological and emotional imperative that drives human pairing despite all rational objection. Oil & Whiskey examines this force through the lens of contemporary ambivalence, where passion and practicality wage perpetual war. The production’s refusal to offer easy answers, its acknowledgment that some loves are better appreciated from a distance, demonstrates a maturity uncommon in the romantic comedy form.

Technical Mastery in Service of Story

Sheridan Glover’s work as technical director deserves particular commendation—the lighting designs created distinct emotional territories within the space’s intimate confines. The transitions between memory and present action, between public performance and private confession, were managed with admirable clarity. In a production where the band occupies the same visual field as the actors, such technical precision becomes essential to narrative coherence.

The ensemble’s energy never flagged across the evening’s two acts, maintaining the kind of commitment that transforms written comedy into lived experience. Audience laughter and audible sympathy—that most honest barometer of theatrical success—remained constant throughout, suggesting that whatever philosophical questions the piece raises, it never forgets its primary obligation to entertain.

A Contemporary Classic in Formation

One departed The Chain Theatre in Manhattan’s Garment District, contemplating not only the specific romantic travails of Zelda and Teddy, but the larger question of how we navigate desire in an age of infinite possibility and perpetual deferral. The production suggests that perhaps the country music tradition—with its unflinching examination of heartbreak, its celebration of resilience, its recognition that some wounds never fully heal—offers as valid a framework for understanding modern love as any contemporary psychological theory.

L-R: Tanner McIntyre, Jater Webb, Isabel Stewart and Levi Penley – the Cast of Oil and Whiskey at the Chain Theatre Photo by Liz Guenther

Oil & Whiskey: A Country Music Meditation on Modern Romance

CAST:

  • Zelda: Isabel Stewart
  • Teddy: Jater Webb
  • Bree: Tanner McIntyre
  • Ray: Levi Penle

ARTISTIC TEAM:

  • Book & Lyrics: Dax Wiley
  • Music: Kit Nolan
  • Director: Adam Jepsen
  • Technical Director: Sheridan Glover
  • Drums: Makani Eliot
  • Guitar/Piano: Andrew Miramonti
  • Bass: Cody Rahn

THEATRE: The Chain Theatre, West 36th Street, Manhattan, New York

TICKETS & INFORMATION

Runtime 80 minutes without intermission. Some adult content.

excerpt.rendered: Oil & Whiskey delivers country-tinged wisdom about love’s beautiful impossibilities with infectious energy, sharp wit, and genuine heart. This spirited ensemble transforms a Lower East Side bar into emotional battlefield and sanctuary alike, proving that sometimes the sweetest romances are those we’re wise enough to leave behind.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

“This is real love.”

Six college sophomores meet for a peer support group in Writer Bella Hathorne’s dark drama, you are seen. Their diversity in majors, personalities, and extraventriculars set them apart, but their shared stress and overwhelming anxiety meet expectations connect them. As high-functioning college students, not only do they have the burden of being the best for their professors, coaches, and parents, but they also grapple with setting themselves apart as they become their own selves. They all want to be seen. To be loved. To claim a place in the world.

Kenzo (Meghan McNeive) is the energy of the group: talkative, positive, and “loves everything. She’s the comic relief throughout this piece, the friend to all, the one that keeps the light shining on each girl. Amber (Olivia Francis) is standoffish; the dark, tortured artist and child prodigy. Sofia (Sara Rosenthal)is naive and kind-hearted; sporting a skirt and prep-girl sweater, she’s part of the college’s soccer team. But she doesn’t seem to quite fit in there. Riley (Emily K Hernandez), is compulsive and paranoid, but her concerns with the growing tightness of the group may not be too left-field. Niamh (Malaika Tinashei) is hesitant, contemplative, and quiet, especially around Laci (Jill Zmolek)–

Laci, group leader (although she insists to be just as equal as the others), is more resourceful in her vulnerability. I realize I don’t know her regrets or personal struggles–but its not right away I make this realization. I too, while hesitant, seem to trust her as the other girls do. As a psychology major that works in the college’s administration, Laci seems to gain information from her work, and the others express unease that Lacey knows a little too much for comfort about her new friends.

I find myself thinking about the first college group I attended over a decade ago; I didn’t feel as though I fit in, although the goal of those where you sit around in a circle is clearly to connect with your peers. I remember it was some religious group that was supposed to be uplifting and a safe space to discuss our struggles. Similar to the girls in you are seen, the purpose of that group was to be seen and heard. Isn’t that what we all want when we’re in the formative years of our lives?

In such a small, intimate space, the set of this piece is resourceful and fluid. An entire bathtub with running water is pushed in and out as the girls begin meeting at Laci’s own apartment, rather than an academic building.

Photo by Lauren Redman

While the girls find friends in each other, Laci becomes more than a friend: a mentor on some dark level, a leader, confident, the commanding but innocent voice telling them what they must do to overcome their pasts. We receive a trigger warning before the production even begins, but several of these moments–how far these girls feel they must go to be seen–could be scenes from a horror movie.

The six girls in this group easily fall into a friendship, but instead of turning on each other or breaking into disagreements and catty fights the way girls seem to do through stories, these girls establish sisterhood. Short clips of each girl’s revealing their weaknesses and anxieties cycle through, giving us opportunity to see each of them a little bit more. These clips begin quick, and progress into longer scenes as the girls transition from simply sharing their roses and thorns of the week, to disclosing their deepest secrets. This peer support group functions a lot like an AA meeting: sharing their secrets about their addictions and anxieties to maintaining a supportive environment that fosters community. But it quickly transforms into a cult. you are seen’s sequences of sisterhood are chilling, dark, and a silent aura envelops the space. I notice I’m suddenly aware of how loud my breathing is; I don’t hear a single person shifting in their chairs. We are suddenly too close to the girls; I suddenly don’t want to see this much of them.

Written by Bella Hathorne. Directed by Emma McGlashen.

FEATURING: Jill Zmolek (Laci), Meghan McNeive (Kenzo), Emily K Hernandez (Riley), Olivia Francis (Amber), Malaika Tinashe (Niamh), Sara Rosenthal (Sofia).

CREATIVE TEAM: Zee Cameron (Lighting Designer), Alysia Homminga (Intimacy Coordinator), Colin Rankin (Sound Designer & Technician).

Murmuration Theatre Co presents you are seen at The Maker’s Space, at The Makers’ Ensemble, 13 Grattan St. #408, Brooklyn, NY 11206, until Oct. 19, 2025.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Little Egg is a breakfast/brunch cafe straddling the border between Crown Heights and Prospect Heights in Brooklyn. It’s a rather small but comfortable establishment that puts off a vibe of familiarity, of a “my-go-to-place.” With white paper table covers and a handful of crayons, a welcoming and friendly staff, and food that is unpretentious and good, it’s a very pleasant atmosphere.

The cafe is being transformed nightly, through November 6, into a sight-specific venue for the play oh, honey. With only 27 seats available per performance in the intimate space, it feels as if you’re eavesdropping in on the diners at the table next to you. Go ahead and listen, but you’ll soon realize that it’s not an easy conversation they’re having.

The idea for the play came from an article in The New York Times about a group of women whose college sons have been accused of rape. They come together once a month, on the first Monday, for lunch. A place chosen as it’s far from their homes so that they won’t be recognized. They meet for support, commiseration, and to complain about their waitress.

Tough subject. Tough play. As one of the characters states about the group, you’re not my friends, “I only meet with you because I can’t talk to anyone else.”

They are each handling their son’s actions and legal charges in their own way, their pain causing them to strike out at the others at times to make themselves feel a little better. Deep down they each understand that and accept it. The personal trauma that they each carry is also not known completely to each character and seeing it in the other helps each to discover and deal with it within themselves.

At times the play steps out of realism and crosses into a different realm. Through a light change and a glowing bowl of soup, it moves into the inner workings of the characters and the trauma that each of them is going through privately. At first, I found this a little off-putting but came to realize how much further we were going in character reveals and appreciated these otherworldly shifts and what they added to the depth of the story.

The play is a bit of a punch in the gut, but worth the discomfort as it looks at the many victims of a traumatic act and how they simultaneously cope and don’t cope with it.

To fortify you for what you’re about to see, each ticket entitles the holder to a mug of tomato soup. Other food is served as well if you wish to order.

Go a little early and get a salad or a piece of pie. It will put you perfectly in the mood for the location of the piece.

 

—–

 

oh, honey was written by Jeana Scotti and directed by Carsen Joenk.

Featuring: Carmen Berkeley, Maia Karo, Dee Pelletier, Jamie Ragusa, and Mara Stephens.
With rotating appearances by Brian McCarthy, Lucas Papaelis, Jesse Pennington, and Ean Sheehy.

Lighting and sound design by Attilio Rigotti, costume design by Iliana Paris.

Through November 6. Tickets HERE.

Little Egg, 657 Washington Avenue Brooklyn, NY 11238

Due to the mature subject matter this play is recommended for ages 16 and above.

Triggers: sexual assault.

title.rendered: Three One-Act Plays by Edward Allan Baker

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

The Circle Festival 2025 created a wonderfully beautiful tribute to the playwright Edward Allan Baker at the AMT Theater with “Three One-Act Plays” by Edward Allan Baker, directed by Ed Bianchi, and curated by Suzanne Di Donna.

Baker took the desperation, the trauma of the lives of the blue collar, and transported them to the stage with hardcore precision and fierce reality. His plays are actor-driven and push the performers to great depths of physical and emotional pain to deal with the complications of love and family, and give them heart-pounding dialogue to work with.

The plays, “Rosemary With Ginger”, “Dolores”, and “Face Divided” are all driven by strong female characters who fight strongly with both themselves and the family members with whom they love.

Photo by Tamar Shemesh

“Rosemary With Ginger” is set in a closed-down diner where Rosemary (Julia Burnier) comes to ask her sister for help because she is about to lose custody of her children. Her alcoholism has taken over and pushes her pain to a violence of words and body, that she lashes out at others. Ginger (Suzanne Di Ronna) does her best to be there for her sister, but knows the truth – she is not fit to be a mother. They go at one another, creating stories that are dramatic and uncomfortable in their ugliness, lies created to top one another in looking to relieve personal pain.

“Dolores” is set in the house of a young wife and mother, Sandra (Ava Bodnar), who is enjoying her day sans husband and children. Her joy is cut short by the arrival of her sister, Dolores (Mira Skye Corbara Korngold), who is looking for a place to hide out from her abusive husband. The truth of their lives, the abuse they both endure, unravels as they argue and yell and push and shove, and in the end, remember that they are truly family, the only thing they really have, and search for how to move forward.

Photo by Tamar Shemesh

In “Face Divided,” we are in an emergency room where Debbie (Sadie Bones) is waiting for her husband (Lucas Wilson) to arrive so that they can both go up and see their daughter, who fell down the basement stairs. Here, the abuse is not between this young couple; they are doing their best, it’s just that Debbie’s best comes with a price.

All three plays deal with abuse, both physical and emotional, and how the characters attempt to construct their lives around it. Baker wrote, “Pain is not only a mind that is closed, but locked.”

All three plays are wonderfully acted, as well as the beautiful choice of music for the evening.

The evening was a touching tribute to Eddie’s life and his work. Upon entering the theater, the back of the stage showed a projection of home movies of Eddie, his family, and friends, all of whom were there that night to celebrate their mentor, their father, their inspiration, their family member, and their friend.

Three One-Act Plays by Edward Allan Baker: ROSEMARY WITH GINGER | DOLORES | FACE DIVIDED Produced by The Actor Launchpad and RJ Theatre Company.

With: Suzanne DiDonna, Julia Burnier, Ava Bodnar, Mira Korngold, Sadie Bones, and Lucas Wilson

Creative Team: Director Ed Bianchi, Set Designer Jeremy Watson, and curator Suzanne Di Donna.

AMT Theater 354 W 45th St, New York, NY 10036

content.rendered:
By David Walters

 

As a performer, when you hear the whole audience oooo and ahhh continuously and make that cringe sound that’s almost like a squeak when they know you’re about to say something that is not going to be good, you know they’re with you. You’ve got them. They’ve crossed the lip of the stage, there is no more fourth wall, and they are taking the trip alongside you. At this point they’re not just an audience, but your friend also going through the journey with you

In Tony Award winner Ari’el Stachels play OTHER, at Greenwich House Theater, the audience is onboard, bags packed, pulled away from the gate, with him from beginning to end and even out into the street long after the house lights have come up and the seats are empty. Completely with him because of his honesty and vulnerability, his warmth and humor.

Having an Israeli mother and a father from Yemen it was always difficult for him to know where he fit in, what box to check under race (other being the only true option) and that label of other followed him throughout his life causing him to change schools multiple times in order to try and redefine who he was creating a new persona that he thought would be right this time.

Having that feeling of always being wrong led him to extreme anxiety, obsessive compulsive disorder, and a voice (named Meredith) in his head chastising and tormenting him continuously. This in turn led him to booze, pot, and pills to try and tamper the effects of this psychosis.

Now this all may sound like a downer of a story, with an outcome where possibly the hero fights his way back to sanity, but that’s not the case here. OTHER goes much deeper than that. Ari’el is presently still in the throes of his anxiety as it manifests in his personal and professional life (outwardly with profuse sweating, inwardly with debilitating anxiety). His sharing of who he is now, and how he got here, with a takeaway of, “I’m still working on it,” feels like a friend confiding in you. A friend that you will treasure at the end of this journey.

What the audience responds to in his story is the bravery, honesty, and the sense that every one of us has those same feelings in various degrees of expression

OTHER is a brave show, an honest show, a human show, and definitely not to be missed. One of the very best autobiographical one-person shows I have ever seen.

—–

OTHER, written by and starring Ari’el Stachel and directed by Tony Taccone.

Scenic design by Afsoon Pajoufar; lighting and projection design by Alexander V. Nichols; and sound design by Madeleine Oldham.

For more information visit www.OtherThePlay.com

The play runs 85 minutes with no intermission at the Greenwich House Theatre (27 Barrow Street) for a strictly limited run to Saturday, December 6.

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

Awake and Sing! is an Odets masterpiece.

It’s the story of the Berger family in the Bronx, 1935, struggling financially, struggling to be happy, or at least be content, struggling to fit in while pretending that it doesn’t matter, struggling with pretty much everything, including what love of family means. A magnificent theatrical journey into what it means to be a part of such a unit, to let go of self for the future of all, and the fight to save self under the weight of sacrifice.

The head of the family, Mom, Bessie Berger (a powerful Debra Walton), believes that her tough love, her strength, her unforgiving personification of motherhood, is the best and only way to run her family. Run them as if they are a group of imbeciles who are unable to navigate their own lives. And the family has fallen into that trap through repetition. Years of the same create personal ineptitude. Dad, Myron (Juan Carlos Diaz), is a victim of his wife’s belief that she is the backbone of the family. Diaz is beautifully quiet and loving and walks with both hands on his back as if to hold himself together. He is demonstrating physically his lack of backbone. His inability to be the “MAN of the HOUSE.” The only son of the family, Ralph (a fabulous Trevor McGhie), is in his first real relationship. It is socially inconvenient and also indefinable. The woman, whom we know only by her phone calls and descriptions from Ralph and his family members, especially Bessie, is vague about her feelings for Ralph, and we gather that at some point is using him. Bessie is pushing her children to marry, love or no love, to get them and the expense of them out of the house. The one who sees it all and understands the constant struggle and daily collapse of his family is granddad, Jacob (the marvelously grounded Gary Sloan). Jacob tries to balance all the distorted emotions and needs of this desperate family with humor and love.

Odets created some strong feminists. Extreme feminists. In Awake and Sing, Hennie (played wonderfully torn between freedom and motherhood by Daisy Wang) walks away from motherhood and her infant, which is in sharp contrast and a rejection of what she sees in her mother, Bessie’s need to believe that she lives a servitude life. That she is the one who, every day, sacrifices all her needs for the needs of her family. All of this victimization the characters bestow on themselves is part of the constant reveal of loss and the daily fight for existence under the pressure of life and the weight of societal norms that Odets wanted to bring to the surface of life in the 1935 depression.

Awake and Sing! is usually performed as a super-realistic play, complete with authentic sets, costumes, sounds, and smells. All of that was stripped away as Sea Dog’s rendition is performed in the chapel of St. George’s Episcopal Church. Although the acoustics were difficult at times due to the soaring ceilings of the space, the staging brought out the true essence, strengths, and vulnerabilities of each character and not trapped in its time, but free to be truly heard.

The bare down minimalist set, the lighting, all art-filled and gorgeous! The performances – beautifully tragic!

Awake and Sing! presented by Sea Dog Theater, is stunning on this theatrical platform of church, religion, and faith. The space will have you gobsmacked. It is gorgeous and otherworldly. Even the travel to the bathrooms will be a new experience.

This is a remarkably creative and crafted production that will have you experiencing this play in a new light.

I left the theatre thinking about accidents, beliefs, blind nearsightedness, and the NEED for struggle for humans to feel grounded.

Sea Dog Theater presents the 90th Anniversary revival of Clifford Odets’ Awake and Sing!, directed by Erwin Maas,

Featuring Juan Carlos Diaz, Christopher J. Domig, Alfred C. Kemp, Trevor McGhie, Sina Pooresmaeil, Gary Sloan, Debra Walton, and Daisy Wang

Creative Team: Director Erwin Maas, Production Designer Guy De Lancey, Sound Designer Fan Zhang, Costume Designer Hanxiao Zhang

Running Time: 100 minutes, no intermission

The performance schedule is Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday at 7:30 pm. Tickets are priced at $55 general, $75 premium, $35 senior, and $25 student, and can be purchased  HERE

A magnificent theatrical journey into what it means to be a part of such a unit, to let go of self for the future of all, and the fight to save self under the weight of sacrifice.
