content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

“Ragtime” is not a musical so much as it is a tsunami, at the center of which is an astonishing talent by the name of Joshua Henry in the role of Coalhouse Walker Jr.  Mr. Henry’s depth and strength envelopes the stage and everyone in the theatre.  Joshua Henry is, in a word, magnificent.  One gets the feeling he could serenade a Radio City Music Hall audience without the aid of a microphone.

I had the honor of reviewing the 2009 production of “Ragtime”  and this incarnation is right up there with its predecessor, but it is a different production in all ways.  While the 2009 production was an intimate and grand opus to people taking care of one another (aided by an extraordinary set design by Derek McLane that is missing here) this production under the direction of Lear DeBessonet,  is spare and focuses on the weaving of the stories.

The story, originally in a book of the same name by E. L. Doctorow, takes place in 1906, at the exact time when New York itself was an intersection point of the very rich, the very poor, and people creating their own entertainment and means of survival.  At the exact time when Ragtime shook the world down to its bones.  Ragtime released the corsets and white ties and reminded people what was at the center of their very being.

In other words – a lot like now.

Because of the nearness of everything in the metropolitan arena, three families – the white folks up in New Rochelle (known only as Mother (Caissie Levy), Father (Colin Donnell), Mother’s Younger Brother (Ben Levi Ross) and The Little Boy (Nick Barrington), the black community in Harlem – led by Walker Jr. , and the widower Tateh from Latvia (Brandon Uranowitz) who is raising his unnamed daughter (Tabitha Lawling) on the Lower East Side – all stumble into each other’s orbits.  And once stumbled, they stay.

Everyone’s lives are sixes and sevens as the tale begins.  Like the world swirling around them.  Sarah (Nichelle Lewis) is a refugee from Harlem.  She flees to New Rochelle to be a domestic and to hide her pregnancy from Coalhouse who is the father.  Her attempt to kill her son fails when the baby is discovered in the Mother’s garden.  Instead of turning Sarah in and surrendering the baby to what social services existed, Mother decides to keep them both.  Because Father is away on an expedition, Mother is the decision maker.  The poop hits the fan later on.

As if by magic, Coalhouse discovers Sarah’s location and learns of his son.  Sarah is wooed until she gives in and the two are united in what everyone hopes will be a happily ever after.

Not so much.

Nichelle Lewis and Joshua Henry; photo by Matthew Murphy

The dreams of this newly minted black couple run afoul of racism, which escalates until it reaches the point of no return.  Like I said – kind of like now.

In fact we cannot watch this story without thinking of the tumult going on outside the theatre.  It occurred to me as I watched that the live arts and the graphic arts may be the only places that the current regime cannot touch because of their very nature.  You can shut down a television show, you can even close a theatre – but theatre will rear up again and again.  Music will still be written.  Poets will still wax poetic.  Here, the music of Flaherty and Ahrens washes over us in great sweet waves that slosh through and around us.  We can feel the tide coming in and going out with each song.  Crying is not obligatory, but it is difficult to avoid.  Starting with the first act when Coalhouse and Sarah erupt with the joy of finding one another again and we rise as one, lifted by their hope and bravery.

Other songs are tempered with the wisdom and loneliness of retrospection, the human connection that crosses social boundaries.  Caissie Levy is breathtaking as she delivers one song after another that trace Mother’s change from a woman depending on her husband to a woman stepping out into the world without apology.

Joshua Henry Caissie Levy Brandon Uranowitz and the company of RAGTIME photo by Matthew-Murphy

“Ragtime” is an operetta in fact and deed.  The story is sung to us.  The spoken words are few and far between.  It is a serenade to the possibilities of life, even when we are mired in tyranny and beaten down by hypocrisy.  Ragtime gives us hope to hold onto today, where hope for most of us is a spare commodity.

Like I said – Ragtime is about today.  If nothing else it will make you remember you are not alone.

RAGTIME – Book by Terrence McNally, based on the novel by E. L. Doctorow; music by Stephen Flaherty; lyrics by Lynn Ahrens

The creative team for the Lincoln Center Theater production of Ragtime includes Terrence McNally (book), Stephen Flaherty and Lynn Ahrens (music and lyrics), Lear DeBessonet (director)

WITH Joshua Henry, Caissie Levy, Brandon Uranowitz, Colin Donnell, Nichelle Lewis, Ben Levi Ross, Shaina Taub, John Clay III, and Rodd Cyrus. Anna Grace Barlow, Nick Barrington, and Tabitha Lawing.

Ensemble members Nicholas Barrón, Lauren Blackman, Briana Carlson-Goodman, Jordan Chin, Billy Cohen, Rheaume Crenshaw, Charity Angél Dawson, Ellie Fishman, Jason Forbach, Ta’Nika Gibson, David Jennings, Kaleb Johnson, Marina Kondo, Morgan Marcell, Kane Emmanuel Miller, Tom Nelis, Kent Overshown, Kayla Pecchioni, John Rapson, Deandre Sevon, Jacob Keith Watson, and Alan Wiggins, Eean Sherrod Cochran, Kerry Conte, Nick Gaswirth, Jackson Parker Gill, Jenny Mollet, Matthew Scott, and Ellie May Sennett.

CREATIVE TEAM:  Ellenore Scott (choreography), David Korins (set design), Linda Cho (costume design), Adam Honoré & Donald Holder (lighting design), Kai Harada (sound design), 59 Studio (projection design), Tom Watson (hair and wig design), Ann James (sensitivity specialist), and The Telsey Office, Craig Burns, CSA (casting). Music Director James Moore will conduct a 28-piece orchestra featuring original orchestrations by William David Brohn, and vocal arrangements by Stephen Flaherty.

 

Through January 4 at Lincoln Center.  Tickets HERE

I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

By Tulis McCall

Everybody’s looking for love in Ethan Coen‘s play “Let’s Love” at Atlantic Theater.  In all the wrong places, in all the right places, who cares?  It’s the search that matters.  Like hunters in a duck blind, they wait.  As for the act of love itself, well that is kind of the center of the corn dog.  Before and after you get to the center there is a lot of dough to conquer.  Speech-a-fyin’ we sometimes call it.  Coen believes in it.  In the penultimate scene one character says to another “Speech is how we conquer death.” which, at the very least is a thought worth examining.

Noah Robbins and Dylan Gelula; Photo by Ahron Foster

I am not certain why this collection of plays IS a collection of plays.  There is no through-line, except for the looking for love part.  It is more like an à la crate menu of offerings that goes by so quickly you forget what came before.

What does connect is the crackerjack talent and skill of every actor on that stage.  From the soft silhouette serenading of Nellie McKay to the sad reminiscences of the Broad (Mary McCann) and The Man (Dion Graham) at the bar, to the wild snap turtle behavior of Susan (Aubrey Plaza),  to unexpected stone cold pronouncements by Tough (Chris Bauer).  These actors never let up.  This is especially true in the scene titled “Brown Eyes” where there is a train wreck of grand proportions (not to mention what sounds like a gigantic metaphor contest) that gets larger and larger with each breath.  I myself laughed out loud more than once – and I am a cranky Yankee who rarely laughs in the theater because I am too busy watching.  This is some hilarious banter.

Don’t go expecting to be wowed by Mr. Coen’s text, but do expect to be wowed by these actors and Neil Pepe‘s direction that serves them and their tales very well indeed.  “Let’s Love!” is engaging without involving you.  I could have used a little more involvement, but I’ll settle for a few laughs delivered by a few pros.

Let’s Love by Ethan Coen and directed by Neil Pepe

WITH Chris Bauer, Dylan Gelula, Dion Graham, Mary McCann, Nellie McKay, Aubrey Plaza, Noah Robbins, CJ Wilson, and Mary Wiseman

Sets by Riccardo Hernandez, costumes by Peggy Schnitzer, original compositions by Nellie McKay,

At Atlantic Theater Company, 336 W. 20th Street, Through NOVEMBER 22.  TICKETS HERE

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Off-off Broadway theater is alive and well at 122CC.

Talking Band’s (winner of 18 Obie Awards) production of Triplicity keeps up their lauded fifty-year history of molding and re-molding what theater can be. Written and composed by Ellen Maddow and directed by Paul Zimet, the play takes on the everyday, the normal, the oft categorized mundane (in other words life) of three people (Amara Granderson, Lizzie Olesker, and Steven Rattazzi) living their lives in NYC, endowing them with a musical score to their musings by Calliope, a whimsical street singer and musician (El Beh).

Incorporating the disciplines of music, dance, and theatricality, Triplicity is three interwoven monologues that reveal the thoughts, fears,  feelings, and desires of our three heroes: a widowed accountant living on Christopher Street, a young writer living with roommates, and an exterminator living with his extended family in a duplex in Bay Ridge. Their lives are connected by threads of a barely perceptible web that seem to drift in the air and only lightly land where they need to be, when they need to be.

As I move around the streets of New York City, and see near a thousand people most every day, I often wonder what are our links, what do we have in common? Besides this brief physical passing, where do our lives connect? They must imperceptibly. Triplicity touched on that connection that we all have just by living together.

In creating the music of the play, the multi-talented El Beh brings a vibrancy to Ms. Maddow’s compositions by pulling a myriad of instruments from a pull cart and singing songs that both accompany and comment on the performers, creating another thread that interwovenly brings the piece its wholeness.

Triplicity combines the mature talents that Talking Band brings to its work elevating the vibrancy of new talent and ideas into an evening that will make you smile, think, and leave the theater looking at the world a little differently.
—–
Triplicity was written and composed by Ellen Maddow and directed by Paul Zimet.
Performers: El Beh, Amara Granderson, Lizzie Olesker, and Steven Rattazzi.

Featureing choreography by Sean Donovan and Brandon Washington. The creative team also includes Anna Kiraly (sets and projections), Mary Ellen Stebbins (lights), and Olivera Gajic (costumes).

Only sixteen performances of Triplicity from October 10–26, 2025, at Mabou Mines at 122CC, located at 150 First Avenue in Manhattan.

The performance schedule is Mondays and Wednesdays – Saturdays at 7pm as well as Sundays at 2pm with an additional 2pm performance on Saturday, October 25. The anticipated running time is 75 minutes with no intermission. General admission tickets are $40 ($30 students, seniors) and can be purchased at www.talkingband.org/triplicity/.

Triplicity is presented in association with Mabou Mines.

Please visit www.talkingband.org to learn more about its 2025-2026 season.

title.rendered: Nothing Can Take You From the Hand of God

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

“I’m homesick and I can’t go home.”

We tell stories, we stretch the truth; but what happens when truth offends those near us? We weave stories, we reshape narratives, these stories become a part of us.

Nothing Can Take You From the Hand of God, starring Jen Tullock, allows us into the memories of its solo performer: a queer author, Frances Reinhardt, who grew up in a Southern Evangelical community.

Tullock plays a host, welcoming Frances to stage; Frances just released her book Never the Twain Shall Meet: Losing God and Finding Myself. At the snap of a camera, Tullock embodies Frances, the author. Tullock’s voice deepens and a southern twang emerges; now she’s one of Frances’s male classmates. Clips of a memories of Frances growing up and again returning to her hometown as an adult, an outsider, literally flash across the stage through Tullock’s performance and across the screens on the stage. A live video records her from all angles. She embodies other figures, including Frances’s own mother, an Evangelical pastor, and Agnieszka, a Polish woman with who Frances claims to have had an affair.

Photo by Maria Baranova

Co-written by Tullock and Frank Winters, Nothing Can Take You From the Hand of God is a piece that focuses on Frances’s upbringing in the church to her leaving it behind; it’s meant for connection–whether its the idea of growing up gay, growing up religious, revisiting trauma through writing and being criticized by it, or, in this case, all of the above. The same stories have been done before, but I wanted this production to really jump out at me. But, alas, Tullock was embodying all these characters–a tremendous feat itself–but there wasn’t justification or evidence behind the words outlined into clips of memories. I felt nothing.

The whips and the welts that made it so hard to sit down in school. The overwhelming religious figures in her life, and the simultaneous longing to hold parts of it tight. While so many details felt so specific and extreme, I found my feelings towards this piece as blurred as the line of what we find to be “truth” in stories we tell.

I want a deeper sense of the longing she has for what she once found in God. I want to feel the home she’s lost.

Photo by Maria Baranova

Audio clips of Frances being interviewed about her book are bridged with scenes of her talking with those from her past. While Tullock’s performance itself is wildly impressive, along with the masterful use of cameras, the story line itself was hazy.

With a large flow of characters only differentiated through voice and sudden, jarring, changes in embodiment from Tullock, I immediately fell off the wagon. I was trying to hold on, to take note of the titles and names appearing on a screen rimming the stage to signify changes in character, place, and time. I would highly recommend digging into context of the play beforehand and understanding the myriad of characters and experiences to that of which Frances introduces us.

Immediately, the set reminded me of The Picture of Dorian Gray: the different camera angles giving off the feeling of a documentary of Frances’s life. The direction of this audio and live video was perhaps much better than the aforementioned Broadway solo show. The creative team and Tullock’s ability to fall into each character so deeply undoubtedly raise the bar for play within solo shows.

While I felt unjustified jabs at the Evangelical community and her upbringing, this work made me not only think about the fine line of rewriting narratives, but the role of people in our stories, and the respect they deserve.

Can two people together in a single moment both have two completely separate truths? The documentation of Frances’s truth is under question. When a story unfolds right in front of us, it’s difficult to not believe it; but when it revolves around a second or third character, it makes me question the rights we have to tell those stories. The gravity that perspective has is relevant. I mean, if truth itself is this fuzzy, then memoir itself can weave into controversy.

Photo by Maria Baranova

NOTHING CAN TAKE YOU FROM THE HAND OF GOD Co-written by Jen Tullock and Frank Winters. Directed by Jared Mezzocchi.

WITH Jen Tullock

CREATIVE TEAM: Emmie Finckel (Scenic Designer), Amith Chandrashaker (Lighting Designer), Evdoxia Ragkou (Sound Designer), and Stefania Bulbarella (Projection and Video Designer). Production Stage Manager: Jenny Kennedy

Nothing Can Take You From the Hand of God has been extended through Nov. 9 at Playwrights Horizons, Peter Jay Sharp Theater (416 West 42nd St, 4th floor). The running time is approximately 70 minutes. Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

There should be a whole set of words for an event that is superb.  “Remarkable” doesn’t cover it.  “Awesome” has been beaten to death.  “Mesmerizing”?  Perhaps.  Still, not quite enough.

“Caroline” by Preston Max Allen and directed by David Cromer deserves every accolade a person can summon up – and more.

When told in a nutshell the story sounds mildly interesting.  A prodigal daughter returns to her parent’s home after an absence of nearly a decade.  When last seen she was putting her family through the wringer because of alcohol and drug abuse.  Today she arrives with a daughter in tow, who has serious issues of her own.  The matriarch is put on the spot about supporting this mother-daughter pair.

See what I mean?

What is difficult to convey is the skill and precision of Allen’s writing.  It is beguiling.  Allen leads us into the story so slowly, that by the time all the variables have tumbled out we are immersed in the depth of the complications.  There are a couple of humdingers of revelations, and I feel compelled to keep them to myself because the manner in which Allen reveals them is near perfection.

Because Allen chooses to move slowly, we are allowed to enter this world (may I give a nod here to the set by Lee Jellinek) that opens up this postage stamp of a stage to reveal restaurants, motels, museums, living rooms, kitchens and a couple I can’t remember.  The changes are simple and swift.  They grease the wheels of the story.  Bravo.

What we don’t see are the breadcrumbs Allen drops along the way.  Under David Cromer’s direction, all three of these women play the card game of “I want what I want.” (Even the youngest, Caroline (River Lipe-Smith) clocking in at 9 years old).  Their positions are laid out like a mosaic whose pieces create images that overlap one another.  Caroline wants to be with her mother, no matter where the trail leads.  Her mother Maddie (Chloë Grace Moretz ) wants that as well, but has experience with the best laid plans going to Hell.   The matriarch, Rhea (Amy Landecker) wants to help both her daughter and granddaughter, but with guardrails.

Chloe Grace Moretz and River Lipe Smith in CAROLINE; Photo by Emilio Madrid

Who gets to decide?  That is the question.

RUN to see this play.  It will make you think, feel, wrestle with and challenge yourself.  You will not be let off the hook.  You will have to dig deep.

This is what theater strives to be.  An event that touches you mentally, physically, emotionally and spiritually.  An event that touches you in places that you didn’t know were touchable.  Happy to report that with “Caroline” the goal is reached and then some.

 CAROLINE by Preston Max Allen, directed by David Cromer

WITH  Amy Landecker, River Lipe-Smith, and Chloë Grace Moretz. 

Caroline features Scenic Design by Lee Jellinek (Oklahoma!), Costume Design by David Hyman (The Sound Inside), Lighting Design by Tyler Micoleau (Buena Vista Social Club), Sound Design by Christopher Darbassie (Camp Siegfried), 

At MCC Theater-  a twice-extended run through Sunday November 16, 2025 at MCC Theater’s Susan & Ronald Frankel Theater (511 W 52nd Street).   TICKETS HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: The Mutables: Bodies That Speak & Minds That Listen

content.rendered:
On a crisp Manhattan evening, the black box of the HERE Arts Center glowed like a living pulse. Inside, a hush spread through the audience—the anticipatory silence before revelation. Then came motion. Five figures emerged, their faces calm as stone, their limbs taut with potential energy. What followed in Kat Mustatea‘s The Mutables was not a performance so much as an awakening—an encounter between human language and the body’s forgotten grammar.

Written and directed by Mustatea, The Mutables fuses choreography, music, and technology into a luminous exploration of how speech and gesture shape consciousness. At its core lies BodyMouth, her invention that transforms movement into phoneme—an instrument through which dancers “speak” by moving, their gestures converted into sound. As each motion flickered into tone and syllable, the boundary between mind and body dissolved. The audience did not merely watch; it listened with its eyes.

ielele — The Feminine Monstrous and the Music of Hurt

The first part, ielele, opened with Marie Lloyd Paspe as NORMAL, a woman negotiating her humanity in the wake of invisible harm. “Am I hurt?” she asked, her voice breaking on its own echo. The question trembled in the air like an unanswered prayer. Her spine coiled and uncoiled with the inward struggle of self-definition. This gesture could have sprung from Martha Graham’s lexicon of contraction and release, where emotion is truth’s first language and movement its confession.

Marie Lloyd Paspe in a scene from The Mutables at the HERE arts center. Photo by Maria Baranova

As the other dancers entered—Rocky Duval, Felix Bryan, Lo Poppy, and Jonathan Colafrancesco—they became the mythical ielele, forest spirits whose voices both enchant and annihilate. Their refrain, “Here I am, hear me,” rippled through Kamala Sankaram‘s electronic score like wind threading through an ancient wood. It was as though the stage had become a neural network of sound and body, each dancer a firing synapse of memory and myth.

L-R: Felix Bryan, Lo Poppy, Jonathan Colafrancesco, and Rocky Duval in A scene from The Mutables at the HERE Arts Center. Photo by Maria Baranova

Lighting designer Christina F. Tang bathed them in reds, beiges, and blacks—colors that flickered like embers of the unsaid. The hues bled into the floor, a chromatic meditation on voice and absence. There were moments when silence carried more meaning than words, echoing Noam Chomsky’s belief that the structures of language—the unseen scaffolds beneath speech—reveal the architecture of thought. Here was the embodiment of syntax: the arc of an arm became a question; a fall became a clause; stillness, the unspoken period at the end of a human sentence.

Rocky Duval in a scene from The Mutables at the HERE arts center. Photo by Maria Baranova

“To Be Heard” — Rage as Resurrection

In To Be Heard, Paspe’s NORMAL struggled to articulate the simplest word: “v-v-voices.” Duval’s ECHO answered, “What if it’s not your voice that’s broken but your will to speak?” The exchange detonated into fury. Percussion thundered; vowels collided. The dancers erupted in a physical protest of the unsayable. Their nearly blank expressions—recalling the icy detachment of Robert Palmer’s famed muses—amplified the subtext: that defiance sometimes hides behind composure, that silence can be louder than screams.

L-R: Lo Poppy, Marie Lloyd Paspe, and Felix Bryan in a scene from The Mutables at the HERE arts center. Photo by Maria Baranov

This was Daniel Nagrin’s philosophy made flesh: that dance is not an adornment but “the body thinking aloud.” Each gesture was cognition in motion, a philosophy translated into breath. The choreography demanded courage; it asked its performers to confront vulnerability not as weakness but as agency. Their discipline was as rigorous as their empathy was raw.

Helicopter — Becoming Furiously New

The second half, Helicopter, burst forth in fog and metallic sound, the dancers transformed into a living engine—breathing, whirring, trembling. Mustatea’s text tells of a woman sprouting blades from her scapulae, as her mother asks, “Who would marry you now?” It’s a myth of metamorphosis, womanhood transfigured through propulsion and pain.

Johathan Colafrancesco in a scene from The Mutables at the HERE arts center. Photo by Maria Baranova

Lo Poppy’s solo embodied the metamorphosis with exquisite tension, each movement slicing the air like a rotor, each breath propelling her closer to transcendence. Across the stage, Felix Bryan answered in rippling counterpoint, his lines both mechanical and human. Jonathan Colafrancesco anchored the motion with quiet gravity, his stillness cutting deeper than frenzy.

Sound designer Jimmy Kavetas layered Sankaram’s score with thrum and pulse—sonic strata that seemed to vibrate within the body itself. Paulina Olivares‘s costumes and Camelia Skikos‘s featured designs merged flesh with fabric, turning skin into syntax. Under Tang’s light, the dancers became living hieroglyphs, spelling out what language cannot.

L-R: Lo Poppy and Marie Lloyd Paspe in a scene from The Mutables at the HERE arts center. Photo by Maria Baranov

In these moments, The Mutables carried the spirit of Leonard Bernstein—not in melody, but in inquiry. Like Bernstein dissecting Mahler or explaining rhythm as the pulse of understanding, Mustatea uses sound not to accompany emotion but to question it. Her performers don’t simply dance to music—they argue with it, philosophize through it. Bernstein once said, “The best way to know a thing is in the context of another discipline.” Here, movement becomes grammar, and sound becomes the logic of feeling.

Language and Liberation

What lingers is The Mutables’ profound empathy. Beneath its sleek technological sheen beats a humanist heart. Mustatea’s choreography turns the politics of voice—its suppression, distortion, reclamation—into poetry. Each gesture becomes a syllable in a collective plea for articulation. When Paspe collapsed into stillness, the room inhaled; when she rose again, we exhaled.

Felix Bryan in a scene from The Mutables at the HERE arts center. Photo by Maria Baranova

Producer Alex Darby and The Hybrid Studio managed the miracle of coherence amid innovation, ensuring the technology served emotion rather than eclipsing it. HERE’s intimacy amplified every tremor; the proximity made each whisper seismic. The work’s philosophical lineage—Graham’s emotional truth, Nagrin’s embodied intellect, Bernstein’s rhythmic reasoning, Chomsky’s structural depth—converged into a singular vision of movement as communication and communication as survival.

The Alchemy of HERE

Since 1993, the HERE Arts Center has championed artists who fuse disciplines into new languages of performance. Its West Village home remains a refuge for those who believe theater can still be radical, intimate, and transformative. In Mustatea’s hands, it became a temple for empathy—an environment where silence resounded, where intellect met instinct in equal measure.

The Mutables is precisely the kind of risk that is audacious, cerebral, and deeply human. It reminds us that innovation isn’t an aesthetic choice but a moral one—the courage to imagine speech where none existed before.

To Be Heard

When the final silence descended, the audience remained motionless, breathing the residue of what had just transpired. To witness The Mutables is to stand where language, sound, and soul intersect—to watch meaning incarnate itself in flesh. It’s a rare evening when art doesn’t just entertain or provoke but teaches us how to listen again.

As the HERE Arts Center ushers in its 2025–26 season, Mustatea’s creation affirms why downtown performance endures: because in the dark, we find the light of shared understanding. In a world of relentless noise, The Mutables whispers the essential truth—
That to move, to breathe, and to be heard is the oldest, and bravest, human art of all. The Mutables transforms movement, sound, and technology into a breathtaking meditation on voice and identity. Through Kat Mustatea‘s visionary choreography and BodyMouth invention, the dancers speak with their bodies, uniting myth and modernity in a luminous call to listen, feel, and reclaim the power of being heard.

THE MUTABLES

Written by Kat Mustatea

ROLES & CAST

PART 1: ielele

NORMAL – Marie Lloyd Paspe
ECHO – Rocky Duval
WIND – Felix Bryan
SUBTEXT – Lo Poppy
FOG – Jonathan Colafrancesco

PART 2: Helicopter

HELICOPTER – Marie Lloyd Paspe, Rocky Duval, Felix Bryan, Lo Poppy, Jonathan Colafrancesco

HELICOPTER VOICEOVER – Kamala Sankaram

Venue and Ticket Information

Experience The Mutables at the HERE Arts Center, 145 Sixth Avenue (entrance on Dominick Street), New York, NY 10013—nestled in Manhattan’s vibrant West Village. For showtimes, events, and the 2025–26 season lineup, visit HERE Arts Center Tickets & Events.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

 

Haunting.

Haunting in its time, and haunting in ours. A warning bell of what’s to come.

In 1934 Sally Carson wrote a fictional novel called Crooked Cross, set in 1933, that dealt with the rise of fascism in Germany, its causes, and where she felt the country was going if it remained unchecked. The book was subsequently turned into a play that ran in Britain in 1935 and again in 1937.

Soon after, her fiction became truth.

With direct parallels to what is happening around us here in the U.S., it’s hard not to imagine our fate is sealed and we’re heading down the same crooked road. Carson’s book is currently having a resurgence and has been republished anew.

The Mint Theater Company is currently running a production of the play at Theatre Row. It’s power in what it’s saying and the warning bell it rings is just as strong today as it was back then.

The title Crooked Cross is in reference to the swastika and its use by the Nazi party. There’s an incident in the play where a giant swastika is set ablaze on a ski slope during New Year’s celebrations. All stand around admiring the pyre and talking about the silliness of the symbol and how it won’t last. Germany is more sensible than that.

The play takes place in a small village in the Bavarian mountains beginning with a family Christmas celebration introducing us to the Kluger family (Katie Firth, Lian Craig), their two sons (Gavin Michaels, Jakob Winter), and daughter Lexa (Ella Stevens) engaged to doctor Moritz Weissmann (Samuel Adams). As the new year dawns we find out that times are tough as the sons can not find work and their frustrations with themselves and the German economy are salved by the messages coming out of the newly formed Nazi party. They end up getting jobs with the party which include new clothes and shoes (brown shirts). As the Nazi party’s hold on the country becomes stronger they become further drawn into the ideology and begin to react and change towards people they’ve known all their lives who are Jewish (their sister’s fiancé being one). Doctor Weissmann ends up losing his job, his home and any hope of a future and tries to call off the wedding. Lexa will have none of it and the couple decides to leave everything and escape over the mountains.

The strength of the play for an audience of today is that it is not preachy and relies on the characters and what they are experiencing to tell its tale and unveil its warning.

—–

Crooked Cross was written by Sally Carson and directed by Jonathan Bank.

This Off-Broadway engagement at Theatre Row through November 1st. , located at 410 West 42nd Street between 9th & 10th Avenues, is a fully accessible venue: all bathrooms are accessible; there is an elevator to all floors; the bar and lounge are fully accessible; assisted listening devices are available.

Mint Theater Company is honored to share that Sally Carson’s novel Crooked Cross, the basis for the upcoming American premiere, is featured in The New Yorker: “The Nineteen-Thirties Novel That’s Become a Surprise Hit in the U.K. Set in a small village in the Bavarian Alps, Sally Carson’s “Crooked Cross” presents an eerily familiar portrait of the rise of fascism,” by Rebecca Mead.

The cast features Samuel Adams, Liam Craig, Katie Firth, Jack Mastrianni, Gavin Michaels, Ben Millspaugh, Douglas Rees, Ella Stevens, and Jakob Winter.

The creative team: Alexander Woodward (scenic design), Hunter Kaczorowski  (costume design), Christian DeAngelis (lighting design), Sean Hagerty (sound design), Chris Fields (prop design),  and Amy  Stoller (dramaturgy).

I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

content.rendered:
By Brittany Crowell

Bullfighting is a dance between human and beast; between life and death.  A traditional Mexican sport from over 500 years ago, the ritual, performative fighting and killing of the bull was recently banned in Mexico City (March 2025) and replaced with a representative performance that caused no harm to the bull.  While the official banning of the sport happened after the play was written, this fight between tradition and evolution is prominent in Monet Hurst-Mendoza’s piece Torera, directed and choreographed by Tatiana Pandiani and currently showing at the WP theater.

In the story, young Elena Maria Ramirez (Jaqueline Guillén) wants to be a Torera, or bullfighter, which is a sport that has been thus far only accepting of men (Toreros).  Her best friend Tanok (Jared Machado) is training with his father and famous Torero, Don Rafael, and Elena follows behind learning every move and mastering them even before Tanuk.  Her mother, Pastora (Elena Hurst), is a maidservant in Don Rafael’s house, cooking and cleaning for their family and helping to raise Tanok alongside Elena.  

Torera focuses on the friendship between Elena and Tanok, their shared dreams, and their different troubles: Tanok has a father with means who can get him into high places, but is harsh and cold; Elena strives to find fame and success in a sport that doesn’t accept her sex and without the financial or political means to get herself there.

Jared Machado and the Company of Torera; photo by Joan Marcus

The chemistry between Guillén and Machado is electrifying and a reason in itself to attend the performance.  As we watch them grow from children to adults, their love for each other and the bantering that manifests from that love endear us further towards the characters of Elena and Tanok and has us rooting for their sustained friendship as well as their shared dreams.  

The scenic design by Emmie Finckel transports us right into Mexico City and provides a playground for the young Elena and Tanok to jump and climb, or a stage for dancing with the bull.  Two dancers, Christian Jesús Galvis and Andrea Soto embody the animals of the sport, becoming dancing bulls and prancing horses and gliding across the stage with their human counterparts.  There is a respect for the corrida (“bullfight”), the skill and training as well as the pride that comes with stepping into the Plaza de Toros; there is also a weight that this carries, which the peace embodies in the loss of loved ones (such as Elena’s father) to the bulls in the ring.

Torera is about the cost of breaking tradition and following your dreams; it’s about deep and long-lasting friendship and how culture and tradition can hold us back, even as we honor them.  It’s at times delightful and at others somber, but overall, it’s a story about love and one that you’re sure to leave the theater contemplating.

 

TORERA – by Money Hurst-Mendoza; directed and choreographed by Tatiana Pandiani

FEATURING: Jorge Cordova; Christian Jesús Galvis; Jacqueline Guillén; Robi Hager; Elena Hurst; Jared Machado; and Andrea Soto.

Scenic design by Emmie Finckel; costumes by Rodrigo Muňoz; lighting by Yuki Nakase Link; sound and composition by G Clausen; props and fabrication by Red Kadetsky; movement and intimacy direction by Carter Gill & Skye Bronfenbrenner; bullfight consultant, Rodrigo Ortiz; casting by Kellie Gillespie, C.S.A.

Presented by WP Theater with The Sol Project, Long Wharf Theater, and Latinx Playwrights Circle. 90 minutes (though run is closer to 2 hours). Through October 19.  https://wptheater.org/show/torera/

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Are The Bennet Girls OK?

Absolutely. As a matter of fact, they’re great!

Launching off the springboard of Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice (P&P)(if you don’t know the story, here’s a synopsis, P&P), and doing a forward one-and-a-half with a triple twist, playwright Emily Breeze superbly executes with practiced form, but doesn’t land in the deep end of Austen’s novel. She instead creates her own beautiful pool to splash into and refocuses on what she deems the core of the novel to be about, the relationship between the five sisters and their mother. This deep pool of fresh water has given her the freedom to release the constraints of language and period style and bring to the stage a delightful retelling of the novel, with a twist or two. There are surprises in the script that step outside of P&P that make a lot of sense and bring a deeper understanding to the character’s choices that have long bewildered many a reader.

What the production has going for it in spades is a true ensemble that plays together really really well. The five daughters (Masha Breeze, Caroline Grogan, Violeta Picayo, Shayvawn Webster, Elyse Steingold), and their mother (Zuzanna Szadkowski), act as a family unit with squabbles, bickering, disliking and liking all in one breath, and a strong love for each other that overrides all the life pressures they are under in the P&P plot. These intimate connections between the actors make for wonderful viewing, laugh out loud funny, and cringingly tragic, truly bringing the audience into what each character is feeling as it is reflected in their sibling.

Edoardo Benzoni, the only male in the cast, plays five men in the story and is a wonderful changeling. With just a switch of an overcoat and physical gesture, he quickly denotes for the audience who he is currently.

Unless you’re unyielding to any re-interpretation of Austen’s work, you’ll have a grand time watching this show and leave with a smile plastered on your face.

I credit director Eric Tucker for expertly bringing this all together, the ensemble, the multi-level staging, incorporating scene changes into the action, and making this a splendid evening watching a new spin on a long held classic of literature.

I also want to give a shout out to lighting designers Eric Southern and Cheyenne Sykes doing a tremendous job in lighting a very difficult thrust stage and creating spaces for the actors to play together, as well as highlighting their moments of intimacy.

—–

Are the Bennet Girls Okay? was written by Emily Breeze and directed by Eric Tucker.

Cast features: Edoardo Benzoni, Masha Breeze, Caroline Campos, Caroline Grogan, Violeta Picayo, Deychen Volino-Gyetsa, Shayvawn Webster, Elyse Steingold, and Zuzanna Szadkowski.

The creative team includes Susannah Millonzi (Choreography), John McDermott (Scenic Design), Buffy Cardoza (Associate Scenic and Props), Mariah Anzaldo Hale (Costumes), Eric Southern and Cheyenne Sykes (Lighting), Eric Tucker (Sound), Caitlin Morley (Associate Director), and Shania Pahuja (Assistant Director), and Christianne Bakewell (Assistant Costume Design).

Now through October 26, at West End Theatre, 263 W. 86th Street.

Tickets to  can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

In Ephraim Sykes’ “Blessings ’N’ Lessons,” Sykes tells his story of becoming an artist, from a young hopeful dancer moving to the Big Apple to a Tony-nominated Broadway actor for his performance as David Ruffin in Ain’t Too Proud: Life of the Temptations. The ups and downs of his journey are told in both story and song, incorporating music from Broadway and beyond. Sykes reminds us that those ups and downs are a part of life, and when that inevitable window closes, another opens to where you are supposed to be. He sings of the positive aspects of the community of theater and the people who live it and breathe it.

Ephraim Sykes is electric, with a soulful voice and spirit that is invigorating and uplifting.

The evening opens with Kendrick Lamar’s “For Free?” (Interlude), which can be a bit surprising to say the least, but immediately grabs your attention. From there, he flips the script and moves to Donny Hathaway’s beautiful and heart-tugging “Flying Easy!”

This was an incredible evening, an energetic, dynamic, soulful blend of jazz, R&B, and funk! Ephraim, with his backup band and singers, takes to the stage with a vigorous, intentional energy that is intoxicating! His voice can do it all! The depth and clarity, the funk and fun, we are in his spell. It was a rock concert of the music of this land. Music and stories were woven together perfectly. He talks of the racism of the arts. “They cast him because they want his color, but they don’t want his blackness.”

From Bruno Mars and Silk Sonic, he sang “Leave the Door Open,” a song about a love that is lost, but the door remains open. As he experienced all of the ups and downs of the theatrical world, Sykes was also dealing with the loss of his love.

There was a great depth and honesty that was shared through his songs and his sharing of the truth of himself. This was one of the most energetic, incredible shows with music that utilizes time and genre that I have had the pleasure of attending.

He had us on our feet dancing that evening, not wanting either Ephraim or the music to stop.

It was a musical, emotional journey telling the story of the life of an artist, and truly, all of us. How we fall. How we get back up. Ephraim reminds us that we can all be the butterfly. Turn from the caterpillar to the butterfly and use our wings to fly. Believe in ourselves. Don’t rely on the outside world to tell us our worth.

He took the drums at one point, and his drum solo was spectacular. He is a musical prodigy! The stage at 54 Below, the entire space, was alive and rocking, following Ephraim Sykes wherever he wanted to take us.

Partnered with Sykes, one of the most connected bands and backup singers, lending their talents to one of the most spectacular performances I have ever been lucky enough to experience at the iconic 54 Below.

Ephraim Sykes and his exquisite band and guest artists are the blessings!  Aramie Payton and D.R. King are tremendous as they, with Sykes, create a trio of sound that is stunning. Featured guest Jennie Harney-Fleming is fabulous!

Go see “Ephraim Sykes: Blessings ‘N’ Lessons” at 54 Below! Only two more performances, on October 7th and the 12th.

Music direction by Manny Houston (Illinoise), and directed by Heather Arnson, with choreography by Darrell Moultrie and Rickey Tripp.

Featuring:

Jasmine Cephas Jones (Hamilton) on Oct 12 only
Jennie Harney-Fleming (A Wonderful World: The Louis Armstrong Musical, The Color Purple, Hamilton) on Oct 2 only
D.R. King (“The Voice”) for all performances
Aramie Payton (The Outsiders, MJ)
Tony Award® winner Adrienne Warren (Tina, The Last Five Years, Shuffle Along…, Bring It On) on Oct 7 only.

Running Time: 90 minutes

54 Below 254 West 54th Street, NYC NY 10019

Premiums are $117.50 (includes $12.50 in fees) – $123 (includes $13 in fees). $25 food & beverage minimum.  Tickets on the day of performance after 4pm are only available by calling (646) 476-3551. All online and phone ticket purchases are subject to fees of 10% of ticket price, plus a $2 facility fee.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

There are a couple of standard rules in the theater which are broken regularly as if they just need to be proven again.  #1) Don’t bring a real infant on stage and #2) No real animals.  The reasons are simple – these darlings will steal focus.  Period.

I hereby add another: Don’t feature a clock on a stage if it is not going to reflect the time or the author’s POV on warping same.

In “Lost And Found” we visit a laundromat in August of 2003.  In case you don’t remember, this is the date of the northeastern blackout.  It affected most of the Northeast as well as up into Ontario.  It lasted a few days as I recall – and I remember that my section of the East Village was the last to come online.  The clock in this Brooklyn Laundromat is preset at 4:09.  To be honest I am not positive that it was preset.  It might have been programmed to STOP at 4:09 because that was the time of the outage.

Map of the blackout with the Northeast in darkness

All I know is that I spent a lot of time looking at that clock and wondering why it was not moving.  There was no power cord.  And I have a clock just like that one – batteries.

So much for distractions.  And distractions are easy to come by when a story that has great potential becomes diluted.  Angelica Gorga found a great nugget for a tale.  Two people stranded in a laundromat when the blackout hits.  One is the manager for a day named Lost (Ivàn Marcel) and the other is a new customer trying to get out of town with some clean clothes that have a story all their own – Found (Angelica Gorga).  Both are waiting for the power to come back on.

What we don’t find out is why they stay in that hotbox of a store.  We also never find out their names – the script refers to them as Lost and Found.  I am guessing here, but it seems to me that the author intentionally left out information as a way of providing clues to the mystery of who these people are and what will become of them – if anything.  After all – life is a crapshoot, and we are always self regulating our experiences.  This chance is too boring.  That one is too risky.  Let’s choose the middle way.  While these two folks do reveal a lot over the course of the 80 minute, the facts feel disconnected.  The revelations don’t stick or add up to a conclusion that makes us care.  The middle way may be real life, but the stage calls for risk.

Everyone feels lost at sea – including the Neighbor (Nelly Saviñon) who has nothing to add to the slow moving story even though she is given the task of trying to right the listing boat near the conclusion.

Like I said this is a heck of an idea for a story.  The blackout threw people together all over the country.  People died.  People were conceived.  Strangers became friends.  Lovers parted.  Lots of possibilities and sparks.  If Gorga returns to this tale I hope she raises the stakes and removes the safety net.

 

LOST AND FOUND, a new play by Angelica Gorga, with direction by Christine Cirker.

The cast for LOST AND FOUND  is Angelica Gorga (FOUND), Ivàn Marcel (LOST) and Nelly Saviñon (NEIGHBOR).

The creative team is  Pauline Walsh (set design), Ryan Randazzo (lighting design), E.B. McKinney (costume and props design), and Kimberly S. O’ Loughlin (sound design). The production stage manager is Annie Beller.

LOST AND FOUND will play the following performance schedule: Tuesday-Saturday at 7pm, Wednesday, Saturday and Sunday at 2pm.

Through October 12 and AMT Theater, 354 West 45th Street .  Tickets HERE

I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs,

BalletX celebrated its 20th anniversary  at the Joyce Theater Sept. 24th – 28th,  presenting a program of exciting ballets, some established and two more recent works, during its all-too-brief residency.  There is indeed much to celebrate. Bold ideas, dazzling debuts — BalletX is always pushing forward, uncovering new delights. This extraordinary ballet company brings together gifted dancers, grounded in classical technique and able to communicate through myriad dance genres.  They operate at a level of skill that makes even the most difficult work look effortless.

On Sept. 24th, the company presented four pieces.  In Scales on the Wings of a Butterfly, which opened the evening, choreographer Noelle Kayser  has wrought a magical world of uniquely beautiful, idiosyncratic gesture and ambulatory movement.   Inspired by microscopic photography, in particular the revelation of the exquisite, painterly detail on butterfly wings,  Kayser has created a whole new dance vocabulary, one that requires technical expertise and sophistication.  And simplicity.  Just as composer Jeff Kolar paints with a wide  array of nuanced natural and electronic ‘instruments’ in his soundscape, so Kayser paints with the dancer’s bodies.  It is an extraordinary, hypnotic work.

Jerard Palazo  brought electricity to the dynamic, bossa nova solo piece Vivir,  in which Choreographer Darrell Grand Moultrie celebrates Latin music and heritage.  Similarly, the ambitious work Sojourner, choreographed by Gregory Dawson  takes its inspiration from jazz  — a musical art form that is at once conversation and collaboration.  In placing players onstage with the dancers, Dawson converses in the present.  Due to its improvisational nature, jazz itself is a living artform.  It welcomes change.  That immediacy creates an exciting dialogue between instrumentalists and dancers.

The dancers entered the stage from the upstage wings, crawling like neophyte creatures around a framework, to spare, edgy, experimental sound, fairly resembling abstract characters in a Heironymous Bosch painting (without the gore).   As the excellent jazz sextet cycled through a diversity of sound, from mysterious and edgy to classic big band, the dancers whirled their way through a  series of ensembles, pas de deux and solos that capitalizes on the exquisite contrast of classical forms, sinuous stretch and modern dance – a BalletX specialty.  Costume Designer Martha Chamberlain’s gossamer designs – billowing shirts, shorts, skirts in shimmery hues of pewter, yellow, tan and white gave the dancers wings, as it were, their billowing hems enhancing the weightlessness of the choreography.

One highlight of the evening, for me, was the excerpt from choreographer Nicola Wills’ gorgeous duet Two People in Love Never Shake Hands.   Wills’ evocative choreography lays out a love story, which we read in the extraordinary dancing of Lanie Jackson and Jared Kelly.  Jackson is lanky and elfin, Kelly compact and muscular, yet they fit together.  The vision of menace Kelly creates with the move of a single shoulder and arch of the back facing his beloved upstage is etched on my memory, as is Jackson’s girlish frisson of delight at his first touch.  As the relationship morphs from excitement at first meeting, to the development of love, its misunderstandings and mishaps, we witness their emotional changes through not just their gesture but the subtle alterations in stance.  The sprite has a steely spine; the strongman a vulnerability that belies his extraordinary musculature.

There is not a weak link in this dance company.  They communicate in every style.  In the midst of a very modern piece – ooh a perfect pirouette – hmm, is that a triple tours?  Why yes.  It is.  This strong foundation in classical training enables these artists to perform the most intricate steps and difficult lifts, freeing them to dance fully immersed in expression.  BalletX moves forward without abandoning the past.  20 years and counting – Bravo BalletX!

BalletX, at the Joyce Theater (175 Eighth Ave.)

In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Will Harrison as Jacob is kept on his toes for the better part of the first act of Punch, by James Graham, now at Manhattan Theatre Club’s Friedman Theatre.  Harrison tears into Jacob’s teenage journey, which is loaded with adrenaline, drinking and drugs.  Jacob maneuvers the through The Meadows (a housing estate outside Nottingham England – what we would call public housing) where he lives among the other teenagers who are lost and uncared for.  We watch and nearly lose our way, as he slams from one pub, or fight, or something that is generally dangerous until he delivers The Punch that does him in.  The punch that fells a bystander and lands Jacob in jail.

This is, however, just the beginning of the tale.  Jacob, we know from the literature and the fact that this play is based on the book that the real life Jacob himself wrote..  This is the story of his fall and his redemption.  Jacob survives and lives to tell the tale.

I am not giving anything away here as it is made plain in the program that this story is a true one.

For my money, however, this story is not about Jacob’s redemption.  It is about the woman who made that possible.  The mother of James, who died after being punched by Jacob.  Joan (Victoria Clark)  and her husband David (Sam Robards) were shattered when their son died.  It was Joan who questioned what the two of them could do to get some answers.  The legal system was cut and dried.  Jacob delivered the punch.  James died.. The end.  Joan, and eventually David, decided that there had to be more that they could do.  They were the victims of the crime as well.  There had to be a way for them to get support.

And there was – not without a boatload of work and dedication.  They found Restorative Justice, and within that group they found counseling that lead them to meet Jacob.

Victoria Clark; photo by Matthew Murphy

And THAT is all because of Joan.  Let me ask you, who among us would ask to meet the person who harmed anyone we loved?  Graham doesn’t lean heavily on the Joan element, and this is an uneven production with accents flying left and right, but Graham does enough to keep a steady hand so that Joan’s struggle, generosity and open heart can be laid out by the delicate work of Clark.  Clark guides us through what is an extraordinary journey that begins with a tragedy and ends up in our laps.

What would we do, the author asks without asking.  What would we do?

PUNCH by James Graham, based on the book “Right From Wrong” by Jacob Dunne, Directed by Adam Penford.

WITH Camila Canó-Flaviá, Victoria Clark, Will Harrison, Cody Kostro, Piter Mareks, Sam Robards, and Lucy Taylor.

The creative team for Punch is Anna Fleischle (Scenic and Costume Design), Robbie Butler (Lighting Design),Alexandra Faye Braithwaite (Original Music & Sound Design), Leanne Pinder (Movement Director), Ben Furey (Dialect Coach), Charlotte Fleck (Dialect Coach),

Manhattan Theatre Club, in association with Nottingham Playhouse, through November 2.  TICKETS.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Art, now playing at Broadway’s Music Box, is a winner. A winner, mostly because of James Corden’s performance as Yvan. His two other performers and personal friends (there’s a palpable connection between these three actors that is evident beyond their characters), Bobby Cannavale and Neil Patrick Harris, are acceptable in their turns, but Mr. Corden has created a character that puts his stardom aside and instead inhabits his role, which makes us forget his notoriety. Not an easy task, but one that he demonstrates he is more than capable of. Playing the historical jester in the threesome, his insight and acceptance of all their true natures is compelling, and to which the audience completely identifies. His monologue about the fiasco of his impending wedding stops the show for its own applause.

Despite what you might have heard, the play is not really about the painting. What it’s really about is unexpressed, long-harbored feelings between friends that have festered for years. These three long-time (15+ years) friends haven’t been able to see each other for some time due to life getting in the way, and finally come together over the extravagant purchase of a modern art painting by one of the group, Serge (Neil Patrick Harris). What bubbles to the surface from the differences of opinion about the work are damning long-held private beliefs about each other that obliterate the foundations of their friendship revealing the shaky ground it has always rested on. The painting is just a catalyst that opens the doors and windows of a deep-seated animosity between the three.

The form of the play is presented in dialogues between mostly two, and sometimes all three, characters, as well as direct audience address, revealing their innermost thoughts. This approach creates a quick intimacy with the audience and each character. Though each actor’s stardom doesn’t hurt with establishing that intimacy.

The set (by David Rockwell) and costumes (by Linda Cho) both rely on a muted gray palette to accentuate the starkness of the painting. This works well.

Broadway revival of the Tony Award-winning ART by Yasmina Reza, translated by Christopher Hampton. Under the direction of Scott Ellis.

Starring Bobby Cannavale, James Corden, and Neil Patrick Harris

Now at Broadway’s Music Box Theatre (239 West 45th Street), New York City. The production will play a limited 17-week engagement through
December 21, 2025.

Kid Harpoon created original music for the production. The design team includes David Rockwell (Set Design), Linda Cho (Costume Design), Jen
Schriever (Lighting Design), and Mikaal Sulaiman (Sound Design).

Tickets are available online at Telecharge, the box office, or by phone at 212-239-6200.

1 hour and 30 minutes with no intermission

@graph.description: 57 years of lovingly working on the craft of theater, what it is, what it means to create it, as well as the diligent process involved in its birthing, has led me to act, write, produce, work every job on crew, and watch from the audience a multitudinous array of offerings that loosely define the word theater. I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Ah!  Would that the title were true!

As we enter the theatre we see a simple setup for a TV interview.  The black chair, the notes, the spotlight.  On the back wall this quote is projected:

“Journalists may write the first draft of history, but dramatists write the last.”Sophocles, 497-406BC

A promising start!

I think the best way to start is by quoting Producer, Eric Krebs who wrote in the program: “The script of Murdoch; The Final Interview came to me in a very strange way,” says Mr. Krebs.  “It was left at the door of Theater555 overnight in a plain manila envelope addressed to me. I looked inside and found a script with a note that said that the playwright wanted to remain anonymous, but that I was welcome to produce the play if I so desired. I thought immediately of “Deep Throat,” the mysterious incident that took place during the Nixon years.  So, of course, I set to work reading the play and discovered a marvelous jigsaw of a drama.”

Indeed – this is a jigsaw puzzle from beginning to end.  Jamie Jackson appears onstage as the TV host of “At The Moment” –  with Chodrum Trepur (an ananym of Rupert Murdoch which is a clue to the ride we are about to take).  He welcomes us all to this most unusual event in which Murdoch will submit to a smattering or questions ranging from the benign to the deeply personal.  In a flash Jackson transforms into Murdoch, complete with the requisite Australian accent.  Murdoch is docile in the first moments of the play, and Jackson is deft at switching from Trepur to Murdoch (as well as a bevy of other characters from family and work).  We settle in.  Murdoch says he does not know why he is doing an interview – which seems off – and Trepur glosses over Murdoch’s confusion.

The plan is to divide up the interview into sux sections – in the same way that Murdoch divided up his newspaper coverage. Page One, the headline, Section Two, local new, Three is international news,Four is business, Five is politics and opinion, Six is Marriage and relationship tips. And finally the back page: letters to the editor.  Murdoch insists the back page was always Sport and Trepur brushes this aside.

We time travel from Australia and a strict upbringing to Murdoch’s stint in London “giving the people what they wanted” and turning newspapers into tabloids and political leaders into Prime Ministers.  Then it was time for the US of A where he made people into Presidents. One by one he maneuvers political leaders to slay the dragons of Citizenship (Reagan) , the Fairness Doctrine (Reagan) and Cross Media Ownership (Clinton).

Voila – Fox News is born.  24 Hours of “The Truth”.

Throughout the interview, as Murdoch changes ages and other characters populate the stage, we get a boatload of quotes that are accurate and disturbing.  “Idealism dies at power’s birth.” “It is the lowest common denominator which unites the largest number of people.”

We watch as Murdoch evolves into a beast that needs to consume more and more in order to satisfy an appetite that keeps on growing.  Until it collapses in on itself under the mighty weight of public responses and Letters To The Editor.

Jackson does great service to all the characters in the saga.  The problem for me was that there were so many of them that I fell off the caboose more than once.  The material is dense, to be sure, and there was no let up until the final-final where Murdoch, in a perfect narcissistic pose, blames us.  It was us he was feeding, not himself.  It was we who devoured everything he consumed.

Shame on us.

An unsatisfactory conclusion to an unsavory tale anout an unbearable man who still walks among us.

Would that there had been a few more cracks in this story’s facade to let in the light.  Darkness doesn’t amount to much without light.  It just repeats itself.

SPECIAL MENTION must be made for  Christine Vega (Standby Assistant Stage Manager) who handled a multitude of props that came and went throughout the 90 minutes.  Her work was seamless.

MURDOCH: The Final Interview, a new American play by an unnamed source, Directed by Christopher Scott.

WITH  Jamie Jackson.

The creative team is Peter R. Feuchtwanger (set design), Joan Racho-Jansen (lighting design), Andy Evan Cohen (audio visuals), Josh Weidenbaum (sound design) and SoHee Youn (music composer).

MURDOCH: The Final Interview will play the following performance schedule: Tuesday – Saturday at  7:30pm and Sunday at 3pm.

Tickets are $49-$79 and may be purchased online here. Tickets may also be purchased in person at the Theater555 box office one (1) hour before curtain.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Trauma stays in the body and long lingers like a shadow caught out of the corner of your eye, just around the corner, just out of sight.

That is what is happening to several characters, Dave and Sonia (Michael Hayden and Samantha Mathis), in the play The Honey Trap, now running at Irish Repertory Theatre. These shadows have been haunting them their whole lives, and the crux of this play is the light now being shed on their personal darknesses.

A honey trap is a “trapper” who forms a romantic or sexual relationship with a “target” to gain access to information, influence, resources, or, in this case, lure them to their untimely murder.

The play centers around the remembering of the assassination of a young British soldier (Harrison Tipping) during the Troubles in Ireland in 1979. An oral history researcher (Molly Ranson) is documenting stories of people from all sides of the conflict who lived through those difficult times and the parts they played in it. While interviewing a British soldier, Dave, his recollection of losing his dear friend and the part he played in it comes roaring into the present, causing him to seek revenge on those he has blamed his whole life (revenge in order to take the heavy personal blame he has been carrying off of himself). He seeks out one of the last survivors, Sonia, and the two face off through a life-and-death struggle to purge their guilt. What is revealed to the audience is how we often have to self-delude to survive.

To live with some of the horrors of being alive, we often lie to ourselves to survive the trauma of it all. Those who don’t, frequently physically harm themselves, as the trauma of what they’ve survived is too much for their souls.

Charlie Corcoran’s set flips easily from past to present, and the use of scrim in the walls points out the porosity of life and memory that the characters experience. Michael Gottlieb’s fluid lighting accentuates the many changing moods throughout the play.

The Honey Trap is another prize, another winner, on Irish Repertory Theatre’s shelf of good historical dramas with deep psychological underpinnings that make for a great night out at the theatre.

—–
The Honey Trap was written by Leo McGann and directed by Matt Torney.
The cast includes Michael Hayden, Doireann Mac Mahon, Daniel Marconi, Samantha Mathis, Molly Ranson, Harrison Tipping, and Annabelle Zasowski.
Set design by Charlie Corcoran, lighting design by Michael Gottlieb, costume design by Sarita Fellows, sound design by James Garver, wig and hair design by Tommy Kurzmanand, and properties by Nicole Rozanski.
Performing in Irish Rep’s Francis J. Greenburger Mainstage (132 West 22nd Street), for a limited run through November 9, 2025.
Tickets can be purchased HERE.
Running time: 2 1/2 hours with one intermission.

@graph.description: 57 years of lovingly working on the craft of theater, what it is, what it means to create it, as well as the diligent process involved in its birthing, has led me to act, write, produce, work every job on crew, and watch from the audience a multitudinous array of offerings that loosely define the word theater. I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

By David Walters
All right. Good night. is at NYU Skirball for ONLY THREE PERFORMANCES, September 25-27.
This is the North American premiere, which has toured major venues worldwide, and New York is lucky to get the chance to experience this performance. But like a firework, it spectacularly explodes, dazzles, and quickly dissipates, leaving emptiness behind. So, if you’re coming across this in time. Go.
You will read, you will watch, you will listen, you will think, you will wonder, you will self-examine, you will question, you will ponder from both within and without. All good things. They are gifts from watching  All right. Good night., and are what makes theater that comes at us from outside the normal lanes so valuable.
The company frames a portion of the large Skirball stage, and with a minimalism of set, an ensemble of five musicians, and two stagehands, sends the audience on a journey of personal discovery, examining what it means to lose someone both physically and mentally, examining what disappearence of someone you love means.
Writer/director Helgard Haug utilizes her theatrical company, Rimini Protokoll, original music by Barbara Morgenstern, and the musical gifts of Zafraan Ensemble to create a piece about loss, tying together two stories, the decline of a father due to dementia, and the sudden unexplained disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 that vanished off the radar flying over the Indian Ocean in 2014. Both stories leave holes that never close for those who are left behind.
Most of the performance requires the audience to read words and sentences projected on scrims and screens in the playing space (allowing the words to float three-dimensionally), describing the too few facts of the disappearance of the plane, the multi-country search to find an answer to the plane’s mystery, and the following eight years of wondering what happened by the relatives of those who went missing.
Mirroring that in the headlines story is the declining due to dementia story of a father and how his family adjusts. The stories are comparable in that people disappear in various ways. One suddenly and one to a slower degree, but disappeared nonetheless.
The show runs two and a half hours with no intermission.

—–

All Right. Good Night, written and directed by Helgard Haug.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
Helgard Haug: Concept, text, direction
Barbara Morgenstern: Composition
Zafraan Ensemble: Orchestra
Johannes Benecke and Mia Rainprechter: Performers
Emma Becker, Evi Filippou, Margot Gödrös, Ruth Reinecke, Mia Rainprechter and Louise Stölting: Recorded voices (for audio collage)
Evi Bauer: Stage Design
Marc Jungreithmeier: Video/Light Design
Peter Breitenbach: Sound Design
Premil Petrović: Conductor
Davor Branimir Vincze: Arranger
Juliane Männel: Dramaturgy
Lisa Homburger: Artistic Collaboration
Christine Ruynat: Costume and Artistic Collaboration Stage Design
Zafraan Ensemble Musicians (Stage): Matthias Badczong (clarinet), Evi Filippou (percussion), Josa Gerhard (violin), Martin Posegga (saxophone), Beltane Ruiz (double bass)
For tix, visit www.nyuskirball.org. $52-92, can be purchased online, or by visiting the box office in person, Tuesday – Saturday from 12:00 pm –  6:00 pm, or by calling 212.998.4941. NYU Skirball is located at 566 LaGuardia Place at Washington Square, New York, New York 10012.
—–
NYU Skirball is one of New York’s less-sung treasures, as it brings in non-mainstream talent from all over the world, sharing stories and art that you cannot find anywhere else. I have never been disappointed by anything I’ve seen there.
This Fall’s 2025 season features Theater In Quarantine; Irish actor Stephen Rea, Norway’s Susie Wang theater company, a dance/theater piece from Belgium’s Ultima Vez, asses.masses, an 8-hour epic event from Canadian artists Patrick Blenkarn and Milton Lim; and My Town, a queer reimagining of Thorton Wilder’s classic by theater artist Jack Ferver.

By Sarah Downs

“Give me back my name!”

“I could have been a contender.”

“Attention must be paid!”

These words ran through my head as I watched John Leguizamo in his play The Other Americans at the Public Theater tear his way into the character of Nelson, the raging, multi-layered, vulnerable, family patriarch trying to get ahead, fighting a system where the ‘haves’ gate-keep their privilege, insuring certain ‘have nots” do not join their ranks.  This especially applies to race, and as a Columbian American, Nelson has certainly faced bias on many levels.  Nelson has greater demons, however.  He is his own worst enemy.  Poor choices have led him to the brink of financial ruin.  His family laundromat business needs an injection of cash, and now.  Quick to deflect fault, he blames outward – this one won’t give me a loan, that one has it in for him, banks discriminate (which they do).  But it can’t just be that.  It can’t always be someone else’s fault.  Nevertheless, Nelson is a shape shifting, wheeler dealer.  He’s so sure he can make it happen — but at what cost?

The play opens with Nelson at his wheeliest – entering his kitchen, double talking away on his cell the phone.  The family is in a small tizzy, preparing for son Nick (an intense, sweetly vulnerable Trey Santiago-Hudson) to return from several months in rehabilitation after a breakdown that forced him to leave college.  Nelson’s wife Patti (a warm Luna Lauren Velez, sparkling, yet steely when necessary) is busy burning food she never burns and trying to keep it together.  Close friends and family are stopping by to help.  Rain threatens the “welcome home” decorations.  That impossible tension of  ‘let’s pretend we’re all better/things will never be the same’ hangs in the air.  As they wait, Nelson drinks and embarks on a long emotional windup.  Alternately playful and pugilistic, Nelson cajoles, dances, bullies.  He can’t sit still.  Nelson is a wire ready to snap, which is exactly what a son still fragile from the trauma that sent him into treatment does not need.  Almost immediately after Nick returns, Nelson is on the ‘when you take over the business’ track, regardless of the fact that Nick may not actually want to do so.  He just can’t leave it alone.  And this is the crux of the matter.  Nelson just can’t stop himself.  As the drama unfolds, what comes to light is truly devastating.  Nelson’s economic house of cards can’t hold a candle to his emotional one.

Leguizamo clearly has as strong a gift for writing as he has for character.  He leavens drama with touches of humor as he paints an unflinching portrait of damage.  Ruben Santiago-Hudson has directed so skillfully you don’t feel it.  It’s as if everything just falls into place naturally.  The cast is excellent, deeply human and believable.  The heartbeat, however is Nelson.  Ferocious and fearless, Leguizamo inhabits the role to the extent you do not see the actor, you see the man.  His every gesture, his blustering bombast, his piercing anger – all of it so real and so heartbreaking.

The Other Americans adds a Latin American family to the canon of the American family play, recontextualizing hallowed dramatic ground of the working man fighting to get ahead, only to find himself falling behind.  Following the American Dream (a/k/a the American Bait-and-Switch), only to realize that, no, that dream is not permitted to everyone.   Lequizamo has written a new classic, bringing the common man archetype into the Hispanic community, revealing both its uniqueness and its universality, because of course Nelson is an uncommon common man, fighting his way to obscurity.  It’s the invisibility that hurts the most.  And for what?

The Other Americans  , written by and starring John Leguizamo; directed by Ruben Santiago-Hudson.

Cast: John Leguizamo, Rosa Evangelina Arredondo, Sarah Nina Hayon, Rebecca Jiménez, Trey Santiago-Hudson, Bradley James Tejeda and Luna Lauren Velez.

Scenic design by Arnulfo Maldonado, costume design by Kara Harmon, lighting design by Jen Schriever, sound design by Justin Ellington, choreography by Lorna Ventura.

At the Public Theater’s Anspacher Theater (425 Lafayette Street, NYC), September 25th through October 26th.  The performance schedule is Tuesday through Sunday at 7:30 p.m., and Saturday and Sunday at 1:30 p.m.  Tickets HERE or visit www publictheater.org, or call 212.967.7555.  Runtime 2 hrs. 15 minutes with one intermission.
