@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

(un)conditional is one of the strongest dramas about personal truths in relationships I’ve seen in a very long time. It’s currently playing at SoHo Playhouse through October 26, 2025. If you are, have been, or hope to be in a relationship longer than three months, I urge you to see it.

Two couples (Kate Abbruzzese and Brooks Brantly, Annalisa Chamberlin and Nathan Darrow) are both in long-term relationships where the male in both parties is comfortable with how they are. The pressure has been building for some time, and it comes out that neither female is content, one with their sexual expression, and the other with having children. The two couples’ relationship difficulties begin separately but surprisingly intersect at a Target store, and they both end up affecting the outcome of each other’s stories.

At different points in the play, both Kate Abbruzzese and Annalisa Chamberlin are given private phone conversations that they excel in, bringing out the truth of their characters that goes much deeper than their words.

Georgia Waehler’s characterization of a seven-year-old child, with Kate and Brooks as parents, was a delight. Her parallel story of confusion in trying to understand the book The Giving Tree illuminated not only her troubled life of growing up in her family, but also shed light on the adult relationship struggles around her.

What impressed me about playwright Ali Keller‘s script is the depth she is able to take her characters to in their explorations of their fears and desires.

Director Ivey Lowe‘s expert guidance with the touchy material was evident and brought out the best in each actor.

A simple but very surprising and versatile all white set by Lindsay Fuori complements the production, with added creative lighting by Kat Morrill, keeping the pace of the production moving despite the many scene changes. A shout-out to the four stagehands who perform a well-rehearsed, rapid choreography of constant shifting from one scene to the next. They deserve a round of applause.

—–

This production of (un)conditional is a world premiere of the 2024 Lighthouse Series that Soho Playhouse annually runs, showcasing New York City talent.

(un)conditional was written by Ali Keller, and directed by Ivey Lowe.

The cast includes Kate Abbruzzese, Brooks Brantly, Annalisa Chamberlin, Nathan Darrow, and Georgia Waehler.

Understudies are Anna Civik and Nick Jordan.

The production team includes Lindsay Fuori (Scenic Design), Kat Mirrill (Light Design), Elliot Yokum (Sound Design), Olivia Vaughn Hern (Costume Design), Emily Hartford (Intimacy Director).

Performances are Mondays at 7pm, Wednesdays – Saturdays at 7pm and Sundays at 5pm. Run time is approximately 90 minutes. Contains sensitive sexual content – 16+ admitted. Tickets are $41.50 – $71.50 (includes fees). To purchase and for more info, visit https://www.sohoplayhouse.com.

*   (un)conditional explores themes of grooming, and sexual and emotional abuse. There is nudity in this performance. There are no physical acts of sex shown on stage. The child character is played by an adult actor in their 20s.

title.rendered: New York in Five Voices: The ASO’s Bryant Park Summer Finale

content.rendered:
On a crystalline September evening, Bryant Park transformed into something more than an outdoor venue. Framed by glass towers that caught the last glow of daylight, the park became a mirror of New York itself—its history, its diversity of voices, its unquenchable spirit—captured in sound. Families spread blankets, couples leaned into one another, and children darted across the grass as the American Symphony Orchestra, under Maestro Leon Botstein, prepared to perform.

The program, fittingly titled New York Profiles, offered more than music. It was a journey through the city’s cultural DNA, each work carrying its own link to New York. Botstein, never content to let music speak in a vacuum, introduced every piece with insight that was both scholarly and accessible, guiding the audience through history, context, and meaning. His commentary, coupled with the orchestra’s radiant playing, turned the evening into a living portrait of New York in five voices.

Maestro Leon Botstein introducing each musical work in a concert entitled New York Profiles by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Julia Perry — A Short Piece for Small Orchestra

The journey began with Julia Perry, whose career traced both triumph and adversity. In 1965, her Short Piece became the first work by an African American woman performed by the New York Philharmonic—a historic achievement largely ignored by critics of the time. Botstein urged the audience to listen for Perry’s bold blend of neoclassical rigor and personal intensity.

The music leapt to life with trumpet scales, angular strings, and syncopated brass punctuated by the shimmer of xylophone. Contrasting sections of vigor and lyricism circled back in rondo-like form, before tightening into a gripping coda. In Bryant Park, Perry’s music resonated as both reclamation and triumph, her voice returning to the city that once received it with indifference.

Percussionists of the American Symphony Orchestra in a concert entitled New York Profiles at Manhattan’s Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Henry Cowell — Hymn and Fuguing Tune No. 10

Cowell’s ties to New York were equally deep. After scandalizing Europe with tone-cluster piano works, he taught at Columbia and the New School, becoming an evangelist for the avant-garde. Yet in his later years, he turned to colonial American hymnody, finding in it a new wellspring of inspiration.

“This piece,” Botstein opined, “is the avant-garde returning home.” Oboe and strings opened with a flowing hymn, followed by a contrapuntal fuguing tune—elegant, supple, and distinctly American. Heard in New York, where innovation and tradition have always collided, Cowell’s music became a parable of reconciliation, proving that modernism can find beauty in its roots.

Ulysses Kay — Joys and Fears from The Quiet One

Kay’s contribution was a portrait of the city itself. His score for the 1948 documentary The Quiet One, filmed in Harlem, accompanied the struggles of a young boy navigating poverty and temptation. “Kay writes not in sentimentality but in empathy,” Botstein explained to the audience.

The orchestra unfolded Kay’s music with luminous grace—long, arching melodies, harmonies rich with inner motion, rhythms pulsing like restless streets. What began as a film score here stood as elegy and prayer, a reminder that New York’s greatest strength lies in its humanity. In the park where strangers sat shoulder to shoulder, Kay’s music felt like homecoming.

Violins of the American Symphony Orchestra in a concert entitled New York Profiles by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Aaron Copland — Appalachian Spring Suite

Although often associated with the frontier, whereupon Botstein quipped, “Copland likely spent little time in Appalachia,” Copland was a Brooklyn native, and Botstein took delight in the irony. “What we think of as the sound of America’s open landscape was shaped in the apartment blocks of New York,” he noted.

The suite began in misty stillness before blossoming into joyful dances and fervent hymns, culminating in the Shaker tune Simple Gifts. Variations swelled into an anthem of affirmation, pastoral imagery transfigured in the heart of Manhattan. In that moment, Copland’s vision returned to its birthplace, recharged with meaning.

Norman Dello Joio — New York Profiles

The evening closed with Norman Dello Joio’s New York Profiles, a work that gave the concert its title. A New Yorker through and through, son of an organist at the Metropolitan Opera, Dello Joio captured the city in four movements: chant-like serenity at The Cloisters; mischief and laughter in The Park; solemn dignity at Grant’s Tomb; and exuberant festivity in Little Italy.

“This is New York itself, in music,” Botstein declared. The orchestra brought the portraits to life—solemn, playful, mournful, exuberant—culminating in a tarantella that swept the audience into celebration.

Epilogue: The City in Sound

As the last notes faded, Bryant Park exhaled. Blankets folded, children gathered, and the city beyond the park seemed momentarily transformed. The evening had traced New York through resilience, reconciliation, empathy, hope, and exuberance, each work a facet of the city’s profile.

Botstein’s eloquent introductions had bound the journey together, ensuring the audience heard not just music but meaning. The concert was less a sequence of works than a single portrait: New York seen through sound.

Low strings of the American Symphony Orchestra in a concert entitled New York Profiles by the American Symphony Orchestra at Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

A Season of Discovery

As the ASO looks to its 2025–26 season, Botstein’s programming promises to continue this spirit of discovery. Rarely heard masterworks will appear beside beloved classics; new collaborations, premieres, and thematic explorations will engage literature, history, and social justice. With venues ranging from Carnegie Hall to the magnificent St. Bart’s and outdoor stages, the ASO remains committed to making exceptional music accessible to all who seek beauty and meaning.

For those who have experienced the magic of Bryant Park, the promise of a full season feels irresistible—an invitation to join a journey of exploration that enriches not only our understanding of music but also of ourselves.

Maestro Leon Botstein describing one of the musical works performed by the American Symphony Orchestra in a program entitled New York Profiles at Manhattan’s Bryant Park. Photo by Edward Kliszus

American Symphony Orchestra

1330 Avenue of the Americas
Suite 23A, New York, NY 10019
212.868.9276
For information and tickets, email info@americansymphony.org, or click HERE.

excerpt.rendered: Under a starlit Manhattan sky that seemed to pulse with invisible harmonies, the American Symphony Orchestra transformed Bryant Park into a cathedral of sound. With Botstein’s guiding words and radiant performances of Perry, Cowell, Kay, Copland, and Dello Joio, the evening became an unforgettable celebration of New York’s musical identity. This free concert embodied the orchestra’s democratic vision, proving once again that great music belongs to everyone.

title.rendered: The Porch on Windy Hill: a new play with old music

content.rendered:
By David Walters

If you ever thought of spending a more than pleasant afternoon with family and friends sitting on a country porch, tapping your toes to the heartfelt sounds of strings and voices reaching back in time to bring forward old tunes in a bluegrass style, I’ve got a show for you. It’s a cold glass full of iced tea, with maybe a slice of tarheel pie on the side, on a still-warm early fall day, looking out to the distant hills where the sunlight’s angle lends them a sharp crispness only found at that time of year.

Granted, any gathering with family and friends will inevitably involve conflict, differences of opinion, and hurt feelings, but the music will bring you together, providing a neutral ground where your voices can blend and find a united harmony.

The Porch on Windy Hill is a touching story (tears on many of the audience’s faces during the last few scenes) about a long-held family misunderstanding over racism, with bluegrass music.

It’s just after Covid lockdown, and a young couple is traveling in an old van as he pursues his doctorate on the evolving of American music through time and ethnic populations. They are stopping at musical venues as they drive through the Southeastern United States. As her unconscious pulls them in a direction she didn’t know she wanted to go, they meet up with her grandfather, estranged for eighteen years, who is a bluegrass player having played with many of the greats. Through their love of the music, they find a way to build a bridge over the chasm that had previously shaped their lives.

The Porch on Windy Hill is a well-acted, well-sung, well-played, beautiful, heartfelt story interlaced with banjo, dulcimer, guitar, harmonica, mandolin, violin, erhu (Chinese fiddle), and jig doll that will make you smile, laugh, tap your feet, and possibly shed a tear. The story and the performer’s musicality can both stand on their own, but together they lift each other to a richer place. This is time well spent at the theater.

Scenic designer Andrew Robinson’s set is not only functionally reminiscent of the screen-doored country porch we all have in our minds, but it is chock-full of sweet little touches of life lived that lend an authenticity to the construct of theatrical scenery and let us in concerning the person who lives there (a bird’s nest tucked in a tiny crevice, an old electric meter on the side of the house, sticks and leaves filling the gutters, a rusted flag holder, an outside bottle opener, numerous stools and arm-less chairs just right for playing instruments you just know have been sat in and played on for years and years). John Salutz’s lighting expertly plays with the realities of the passing of a day as well as seamlessly and theatrically highlighting actors in their emotional and quiet moments.

——-

This award-winning show, The Porch on Windy Hill, was conceived and directed by Sherry Stregack Lutken.

Written by Sherry Stregack Lutken, Lisa Helmi Johanson, Morgan Morse, and David M. Lutken.

Cast: Tora Nogami Alexander, David M. Lutken, and Morgan Morse.

Creative team: Music Director David M. Lutken, Scenic and tech designer/director Andrew Robinson, Lighting Designer John Salutz, Sound Designer Sun Hee Kil, Costume Designer Grace Jeon.

Now through October 11, 2025 at Urban Stages, 259 West 30th Street, NYC 10001

Tickets can be found HERE.

@graph.description: 57 years of lovingly working on the craft of theater, what it is, what it means to create it, as well as the diligent process involved in its birthing, has led me to act, write, produce, work every job on crew, and watch from the audience a multitudinous array of offerings that loosely define the word theater. I'm still enthralled by its gifts and process. I will endeavor to let you know whether I feel you should spend your time and money, acknowledging and rejoicing in artistic level and effort as a consideration. Thus, I may give a higher mark to the heart and soul of a college production than a Broadway show, holding each to a different standard. As always, just one man's opinion in a world filled with them.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

“Uh-oh… It’s begun.”

We’re in Fresno, CA, and the county is on fire. Preppy-aesthetic Weather Girl, Stacey Gross (Julia McDermott), is on air and on a never-ending bender of alcohol and place attachment. She’s been taught to always smile on camera: through heat waves, while reporting live from a Coalinga field, where a house is ablaze behind her, even when firefighters run out of water.

“I guess you don’t really think about miracles until you need one and this place needs one…”

Stacey is supposed to be a beautiful, uplifting wave of energy. And physically she is exactly that–a perpetual, whitened smile–“because they tell you that’s how you get through these things.” But her mental state is very opposite from this on-screen character. Even her trendy Stanley is a lie: filled with Prosecco to ease her pain.

Julia McDermott as Stacey Gross. Photo by Emilio Madrid

Like previous productions at St. Ann’s Warehouse, Weather Girl, written by Brian Watkins and directed by Tyne Rafaeli, embodies the darkness and unforgiving truth of reality.

It’s 4am, and the fires are getting closer, “like sin coming into the world.” 4am is when we’re most restless, occupied by alcohol, or regret, or premonition; or all three. This cycle of time reminds us of the environment’s increasing intensity and the foreboding, relentless climate change.

But we only want good news.

The audience immediately falls victim to our distorted perception of reality, as Stacey moves to her green screen, wearing a tight, bright pink skirt, red frilly, low cut blouse, blown-out hair and heavy makeup. As the show itself is advertised, it’s “a dizzying rampage into the soul of American Strangeness.”

Weather Girl emphasizes the alternate reality in which we must live if we allow our planet to diminsh at this rate. While Stacey’s date with “Mark,”  “tech bro” is laughably stereotypical and even self-deprecating, it’s equally observational and real.  Ignorant to how he’s destroying the world, Stacey wishes there were people out there trying to find more water instead of ftrying to fit more people.

McDermott speaks into the various microphones on stage to not only communicate the dire weather in levity but to release her own years of trauma. We watch this Weather Girl spiral into a car wreck, waking up in a homeless encampment, clubbing, and driving past the same field where chilling memories have been embed. The lighting, by Isabella Byrd, masters these scene changes as we move throughout Fresno County, Stacey remaining in front of that green screen.

McDermott’s performance is raw and darkly humorous. The absurd juxtaposition of lines from start til end, leaves the audience  laughing nonstop, and I am in awe at how McDermott is able to deliver each, such as the following, while garnering utter laughter on a topic of such despair.

“One day a family burned inside a house behind me and then I ate a chimichanga.”

This is the moment the reality of this play hits me. Suddenly, I’m thinking about the role reporters play in communicating news, their trauma, the enormous emotional intelligence necessary as a “weather girl.” The calm persona they must maintain in high-pressure situations. The trauma Stacey holds from her own absent mother and the resurfacing of her throughout the piece, expectations as a single woman dating, the pressures in the workplace, and longing for safety in her hometown are forced to be placed on the backburner.

Being a Weather Girl is numbing. Until it isn’t; until even the Stanley mug filled with Prosecco can’t consume her the way she needs to be consumed to get through the lies she tells her beloved community.

In search for understanding of her homeless mother and her own magnetic pull to Fresno, this Weather Girl offers much more to anticipate than just the Friday Forecast.

Julia McDermott as Stacey Gross. Photo by Emilio Madrid

“I’m a fluffer, I’ma hype man, I’m a used car salesman selling a world we can’t even have.”

Are we actually the aliens? 

 

Written by Brian Watkins; Directed by Tyne Rafaeli.

STARRING: Julia McDermott.

CREATIVE TEAM: Isabella Byrd (Set & Lighting Design), Rachel Dainer-Best (Costume Designer), Kieran Lucas (Sound Designer), Jack Boissieux (Production Manager), Adam Coy (Associate Director), Emily Schmit (Associate Set & Lighting Designer), Matt Otto (Associate Sound Designer).

Weather Girl is playing at St. Ann’s Warehouse, 45 Water Street, Brooklyn, until Oct 12. Tickets can be purchased here.

Running time is 70 minutes with no intermission.

Please note this production contains haze and flashing lights. Ages 13+ are recommended for admission. No one under age 5 is permitted at the performance.

St. Ann’s Warehouse presents this Francesca Moody Production following Weather Girl’s sold out run at the SoHo Theater in London and Edinburgh Fringe Festival where it won multiple awards including Winner of the Scotsman’s Fringe First Award and The BBC Popcorn Award.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Saturday Church, now at New York Theatre Workshop, is an invitation into a fantasy.  We are invited in by the Black Jesus (J. Harrison Ghee) whose voice and presentation are so smooth that we would follow this holy person a-n-y-w-h-e-r-e.

… you’re about to have the time of your life…can I show y’all what collective love looks like? What collective joy looks like? What collective healing looks like?

Everyone in the audience says yes to this, because who is not in need of some love and healing.

We are not disappointed.  In a nanosecond the Black Jesus is joined by a bevy of dancers/singers whose talents are so superb these folks nearly achieve lift-off.  The first 25 minutes of this show lift us all up, as is the intention.

The company of NYTW’s SATURDAY CHURCH, photo by Marc J. Franklin

What happens after this introduction does not quite rise as high. Not for lack of talent.

This case features TWO Tony Award Winners: J. Harrison Ghee (Some Like It Hot) who performs double duty as Black Jesus and Pastor Lewis, and Joaquina Kalukango (Paradise Square) as Aunt Rose.  And then there are the many nominations  – like Pulitzers and WGA awards – the list is endless.  What we have on this stage is a mighty, mighty powerhouse ready to tell the story of one Ulysses (Bryson Battle – who in real life is a recent college graduate blessed with a voice from Heaven).

Ulysses story is simple: he is torn between two world – the one in which he grew  up under the watchful eye of Aunt Rose and his mother Amara (Kristolyn Lloyd).  Amara is recently widowed and working two jobs.  Barely has time to sleep.  Aunt Rose is mourning her brother, and has taken over his position as the local choir conductor at Pastor Lewis’s church.  Ulysses is desperate to join the choir because he sees it as another family, and this is a deeply religious young man.

His “ways”, however make him ineligible to join.  When he gets caught up in the spirit he gets “flouncy”.  He is “noticeable” and that is dangerous.  Aunt Rose is no pushover and Ulysses ways will not be tolerated.  Period.  I repeat – his ways are dangerous.

On the other side of the coin Ulysses discovers Saturday Church through a passing connection on the subway.  Raymond (Jackson Kanawha Perry) makes his intentions known and Ulysses is drawn in.  Ulysses has not admitted he is gay, although everyone else seems to get it, including Black Jesus.

It takes us a long time – a very long time – for Ulysses to make it to Saturday Church and allow himself to be welcomed and cared for.

Thus begins the trouble.  How does he combine these two worlds?  One is strict.  He knows he is loved, but there are limitations and he must do as  he is told.  The other is an open doorway, but that may lead him away from  his family.

This is a classic and terrific set up for a story.  Either way Ulysses goes there may be loss.  This is where the double casting of Ghee as Black Jesus and Pastor Lewis is a brilliant move.  Both want the best for Ulysses, but one is tied to a narrow perspective and one is ready to untie Ulysses’ wings.  Gee hits both opposing sides dead center.  He is an immaculate performer and brings us into holy grace, as well as the mortal coil, with a gentle touch.  He is an extraordinary guide.

The book and music for Saturday Church are the elements that tend to make the proceedings drag.  This audience is smart, and we get where the story is going within a few minutes of the curtain rising.  For some reason the authors have chosen to stretch the story out when brevity could easily have been the wiser choice.  The audience loses interest in the tale early on – and what keeps us in our seats is the talent and commitment of this ensemble.

This ensemble creates a church all their own and throws the doors open for us.

Of course we accept the invitation.  That is the eternal gift of theatre.

Saturday Church – book and additional lyrics by Damon Cardasis and James Ijames. Directed by Whitney White, with music and lyrics from Sia, and additional music by Honey Dijon. 

WITH: Anania, Primo Thee Ballerino, Bryson Battle, Veyonce Deleon, Michael Samarie George, J. Harrison Ghee, J Quay Gibbs, Fernell Hogan, Dava Huesca, Oyoyo Joi, Joaquina Kalukango, Kristolyn Lloyd, Kareem Marsh, Jackson Kanawha Perry, Caleb Quezon, B Noel Thomas, Damani Van Rensalier, Wade Watson

Music supervision, orchestrations and arrangements by Jason Michael Webb and  Luke Solomon, and choreography by Darrell Grand Moultrie. It is conceived for the stage and based on the Spring Pictures movie written and directed by Cardasis. 

Scenic design by David Zinn, costume design by Qween Jean, lighting design by Adam Honoré, sound design by Gareth Owen, and hair & wig design by Darius Thomas. Music direction by Deah Love Harriott, with music production by Chris Penny.

At New York Theatre Workshop through October 19.  TICKETS

Saturday Church is produced by special arrangement with Tim Levy and Cindy Tolan. 

Details regarding initial events for the Saturday Church FOR THE CULTURE series are available at nytw.org/community/for-the-culture. 

The performance schedule for Saturday Church is as follows: 

  • Through September 28: Tuesday-Friday at 7pm; Saturday & Sunday at 2pm and 7:30pm. Exceptions: there will be no public performances on Sunday September 14. 
  • Beginning September 30: Tuesday at 7pm; Wednesday at 2pm & 7:30pm, Thursday-Friday at 7pm; Saturday at 2pm & 7:30pm; Sunday at 2pm. Exceptions: there will be no 2pm performance on Wednesday October 8.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
Review by Brittany Crowell

“Can you be Black and not perform?”  rings out towards the top of the piece to set the stage (quite literally, as a rolling rack with the question penned in pink LED strip lighting rolls out) for THE ESSENTIALISN’T, Eisa Davis’ new show at HERE Arts Center, a co-production between HERE and The Movement Theater.

Guests entering the theater are invited to walk through a small gallery where the idea of identity begins to be explored.  You then pass through a portal in the gallery to be seated for the performance, already setting up the notion that the artist and artwork is a piece of art, and has been curated and created with intention and influence.

For the next hour and a half, Eisa Davis and her two co-performers, Jamella Cross and Princess Jacob, explore the notion of performance on Black women’s bodies.  They sing, dance, laugh, and connect with each other, bringing the personal and intimate to the public stage, in an associative mixtape which combines ritual and requiem with pop culture and Black history.
The piece draws its own logic and feels real and intimate as our performers share vulnerabilities with us in their practice of exploring how to not perform, in society or on the stage.

The piece doesn’t meet expectations, but its aim is not to. The Essentialisn’t breaks down the constructs of performance in theater in order to explore the bigger role that performance plays in the lives of those classified and identified in a certain way by society.

Essentialism is the philosophical notion that people who are a part of distinct categories are defined by an essence, which separates them from others, and makes them align categorically.  Through much more than name, Eisa Davis’ piece explores and rejects this notion the essential-isn’t necessary; an essence, expectation, and preconceived notion of who someone should be is limiting and leads to folks having to perform these roles in order to feel safe in the world.

THE ESSENTIALISN’T is powerful and restorative.  It explores themes of slavery, repression, obligation, and harm, while creating rituals of music, dance, pedestrian activity, and theater to cleanse the performers and the audience alike in order to build a future of emancipation, freedom of expression, and truth without performance.  The piece begins with Davis’ tenuous exploration of a water tank on the stage and ends with her celebrating and splashing through the same tank in a beautifully wet ritual cleansing.

THE ESSENTIALISN’T brings the notion of theater beyond plays and performances and creates a genre-defying experience: part litmus test, part ancient ritual.  No matter your background or the category which “Essentialism may” place you, THE ESSENTIALISN’T has the power to heal, to teach, and absolutely to entertain.

 

 

THE ESSENTIALISN’T – creative, performed, and directed by Eisa Davis

FEATURING: Jamelia Cross & Princess Jacob

Lighting designer, Cha See; scenic and costume consultant, Peter Born;  Dayeon Jeong; guiding voice of W.E.B. DuBois, Daniel Alexander Jones; Presented by HERE: Jesse Cameron Alick, Annalisa Dias, Lanxing Fu, Lauren Miller, co-cirectors & The Movement Theater Company. Through September 28 at HERE Arts Center (145 6th Avenue). https://here.org/shows/the-essentialisnt/

title.rendered: Rococo Repast: Where Time Dissolves and Music Transcends

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

The American Classical Orchestra’s “Rococo Repast” salon concert at the Metropolitan Club delivered an exquisite evening of period-authentic chamber music that transported audiences directly into the elegant musical salons of 18th-century aristocracy, proving once again that historical performance practice isn’t a mere academic exercise—it’s sonic time travel.

In the hushed grandeur of the Metropolitan Club’s library, where leather-bound volumes line mahogany shelves like silent witnesses to centuries of intellectual discourse, something rather magical unfolded on September 16th. The American Classical Orchestra, under the sagacious guidance of founder and conductor Thomas Crawford, presented “Rococo Repast”—a salon concert that achieved a moment when past and present dissolved into pure musical experience.

Thomas Crawford, Founder and Artistic Director of the American Classical Orchestra. Courtesy aconyc.org

The Perfect Marriage of Venue and Vision

The choice of venue proved nothing short of inspired. The Metropolitan Club’s library, with its soaring ceilings and intimate alcoves, perfectly evoked the palatial music rooms where these works originally bloomed. Founded in 1891 by J.P. Morgan and designed by Stanford White, this architectural jewel on Fifth Avenue provided precisely the sophisticated ambiance that Johann Christian Bach, Michael Haydn, and Mozart would have recognized. Moreover, the acoustic properties of the room—neither too reverberant nor too dry—allowed the subtle timbres of period instruments to speak with crystalline clarity.

Crawford’s vision of historical authenticity extends far beyond mere antiquarian interest. As he noted in his characteristically witty pre-concert remarks, the evening represented what I call sophisticated time travel—an opportunity to hear these works as their creators intended, performed on instruments with period-appropriate features that create the inherently natural blend that scholars of baroque music call for.

Featured Artists David Dickey (Oboe) and Melanie Williams (Flute), in performance at the American Classical Orchestra’s concert Rococo Repast at the Metropolitan Club. Photo of David Dickey by Vlad-Nabat. Photo of Melanie Williams Courtesy aconyc.org

A Journey Through the Rococo Transition

The program itself revealed Crawford’s deep understanding of this pivotal transitional period between the Baroque and Classical eras. Indeed, the evening’s repertoire illuminated what musicologist Harold Schonberg once described as music’s capacity to capture “the very essence of an age’s aspirations and anxieties.”

Johann Christian Bach: Bridging Two Worlds

The opening Johann Christian Bach Quintet in D Major, Op. 22, performed with delightful aplomb, demonstrated precisely why this youngest Bach son was called the “London Bach.” The work’s galant style, with its elegant melodic lines and sophisticated harmonic progressions, served as a perfect aperture to the evening’s exploration. Aisslinn Nosky, whose fearsome, powerful musicianship has earned acclaim, led the ensemble with her characteristic blend of technical precision and interpretive insight. Her violin sang with the kind of warmth that only gut strings and true artistry can provide, creating delighted intones that link the high Baroque to the emerging Classical style.

The quintet’s first movement, Allegro, sparkled with conversational interplay between the instruments, while the Andantino revealed the emotional depth that would soon flourish in his brother’s symphonic works. David Dickey, principal oboist of Boston Baroque, contributed what Crawford deliciously described as “stentorian” oboe commentary that punctuated the musical discourse with authority and grace. The final Allegro assai bubbled with the kind of effervescent joy that made late 18th-century audiences fall in love with this emerging style.

Johann Christian Bach 1735-1782, portrait painted by Pompeo Girolamo Batoni. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Michael Haydn: The Forgotten Master Revealed

Perhaps the evening’s most significant revelation came with Michael Haydn’s Quintet in C Major, MH 187—a work that deserves far wider recognition. Too often overshadowed by his illustrious brother Joseph, Michael Haydn’s compositional voice emerged here as distinctly individual and compelling. The opening Allegro spiritoso crackled with rhythmic vitality, while the Adagio cantabile showcased the ensemble’s capacity for sustained, singing lines that seemed to float in the library’s refined atmosphere.

Michael Haydn (1737-1806). Lithograph by Franz Eybl (cropped), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Mozart: Wit and Genius Unveiled

The evening’s culmination, Mozart’s Flute Quartet No. 4 in A Major, K. 298, offered both challenges and rewards in equal measure. Crawford’s introductory commentary brilliantly prepared the audience for Mozart’s exquisite artistry and sense of humor, particularly evident in Mozart’s playful instructions to the original performers, and the work’s lighthearted dialogue between flute and strings.

The opening Andante unfolded like a sophisticated conversation in a drawing room, with Williams’s flute offering gentle observations that the strings enthusiastically embraced and elaborated. The Menuetto revealed Mozart’s genius for transforming conventional forms with unexpected harmonic turns and rhythmic surprises. However, it was in the concluding Rondeau: Allegretto that the ensemble’s chemistry became most visible and apparent—the kind of musical communication that transcends technical execution to achieve true artistic communion.

Maria Anna (Nannerl), Wolfgang, Anna Maria (medallion), and Leopold Mozart. By Johann Nepomuk Della Croce, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

The Alchemy of Period Performance

What distinguished this performance from conventional chamber music concerts was the transformative power of period instruments and historically informed performance practice. The gut strings, combined with informed artists and techniques, provided a warmth and resonance that steel strings cannot match. At the same time, the timbre of the period flute and oboe created an intimacy that modern instruments often sacrifice for projection. As recent scholarship in classical music performance has demonstrated, these subtle differences in timbre and attack create an entirely different sonic landscape—one that allows audiences to hear familiar works with fresh ears.

The musicians themselves seemed liberated by these period instruments, their natural resonance characteristics encouraging the kind of musical breathing and phrasing that characterized 18th-century performance practice. There were moments—particularly in the slower movements—where time seemed suspended, where the cotton wool of everyday experience dissolved into pure musical consciousness.

Crawford’s Pedagogical Mastery

Crawford’s decision to have performers demonstrate segments of each work proved remarkably effective, allowing audiences to grasp the intricate relationships between themes, melodic lines, and harmonic progressions. This pedagogical approach reflects the broader educational mission that has earned the ACO recognition from the National Endowment for the Arts and positioned it as New York’s leading period instrument orchestra.

The Sublime in the Intimate

What emerged from this evening was proof that chamber music, when performed with such commitment to historical authenticity and musical excellence, can achieve what Leonard Bernstein called “the sublime in the everyday.” The library setting, the period instruments, and the musicians’ evident passion for this repertoire combined to create an experience that was simultaneously educational and transcendent.

The visible chemistry among the performers evoked the social aspects of 18th-century music-making when chamber music served not merely as entertainment but as a sophisticated discourse among equals. These were not simply virtuosic powerhouses displaying technical prowess, but musical partners engaged in the kind of intimate conversation that chamber music was designed to facilitate.

Poster for the 1960 film The Time Machine by Reynold Brown, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

A Testament to Musical Time Travel

As the final notes of Mozart’s Rondeau dissolved into the library’s reverent silence, one was struck by the evening’s deeper achievement. This was more than a concert—it was a demonstration of music’s capacity to collapse temporal boundaries, to make the past vividly present through the alchemy of sound. The American Classical Orchestra’s commitment to period authenticity serves not merely academic interest, but the profound human need to connect across centuries through shared artistic experiences.

For those who experienced this marvelous evening of superb chamber music, the takeaway was clear: historical performance practice isn’t about recreating museum pieces, but about breathing new life into masterworks by performing them as their creators intended. In an age of increasing technological mediation, events like “Rococo Repast” remind us of music’s essential humanity—its capacity to create what has been called direct communication from one soul to another.

The American Classical Orchestra’s upcoming 2025-26 season promises more such revelations, and if “Rococo Repast” is any indication, audiences are in for a series of transformative musical encounters that honor the past while speaking directly to contemporary sensibilities.

For those inspired to explore the world of period performance and baroque music, the American Classical Orchestra continues its season with equally compelling programs at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall and other intimate venues throughout New York City.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Having created and performed together for over thirty years, the singer-songwriter duo of Anya Turner and Robert Grusecki (with Tod Hedrick on bass) has put together a cabaret performance featuring both older and newer work, entitled Joy & Love — a title that reflects their large body of work as well as themselves. They have several more performance dates lined up at Sid Gold’s Request Room in Chelsea, 165 West 26th Street, Tuesdays, October 14th, and November 11th.

Smart, with an underplayed sense of funny, satirical at times, reflective, and exploratory are but a few words to describe their writing, her singing, and his piano and vocal accompaniment. There’s a feeling of being in good hands from the very start, and that is carried through the entire set.

The songs of the evening were presented as themes on self-reflection and secrets (in all their forms), and shed light on both the duo and the things in the world that have caught their interest. There are a number of songs that get their creative beginnings from other people’s lives (Mary Cassatt, Deborah Wood, Helen Gallagher, Billy Tipton, Virginia Woolf, Gladys Bentley, Emily Dickinson). Go ahead and click on some of the links if you don’t know the people they reference. Enlightening, not just for who they were/are, but also who Anya and Robert are, and the well into which they dip, utilizing the bucket of their creativity to bring up treasure. What comes of these explorations is an original authenticity that is relatable, inspiring, and just good music.

One of their more personal songs, “That’s Why I Love You” (from their 2022 CD In This Raggedy Time), has a lyric, “Always fresh. Never old. You are the pounding of my heart.” It reflects the beginnings of their coming together as a couple, both fresh out of school, at one of their first professional gigs that happened to be in Minneapolis, and the glue that has held their partnership, both on and off the cabaret stage, together. It’s that personal care and outlook, with themselves as well as with us, their audience, that makes an evening spent with Anya and Robert a delight.

—–

Joy & Love, written and performed by Anya Turner and Robert Grusecki, will be performing at Sid Gold’s Request Room on October 14 and November 11.

Doors open at 7 for a 7:30 show. $15 cash at the door and a 2-drink minimum.

Reservations can be had HERE closer to performance dates.

By Victoria L. Dammer

Jail, where misfits gather to plot their futures, bemoan their past transgressions, and secure unlikely friendships, sets the stage for the comical play Can’t Run Can’t Dance, written by actor Gregg Henry.

It’s Christmas time on the Olympic Peninsula. We encounter Squeak (Juliet Brett), a high-octane woman in her 20s, who jumps into a diatribe about the turn of events that landed her in jail. She was roaming the streets of Venice Beach and became involved in a brawl with a guy swinging and punching. Her current cellmate, Ingrid (Tracie Lockwood), is a rugged woman who fearlessly tangles with the guy, throws a few punches of her own, and the cops pick them up. Somehow, they traveled north, landing in jail again.

Ingrid has a shady boyfriend named Ronnie (John Stout Adams), a wheeler-dealer with a scheme to make a fortune. They tried their hand at gambling at the Indian casino, but Squeak reminded Ingrid she’s down a couple of hundred bucks. She’s willing to try whatever Ronnie has in mind.

“Hustles change,” says Ingrid, “You gotta change with ‘em. Ride the wave.”

Ronnie is paranoid that the cops and bookies are following them from LA. He’s a conspiracy theorist as well. He’s not happy that Ingrid has brought along a friend to be involved in the caper. His paranoia gets out of control, but Ingrid convinces him Squeak is the real hustler of the three of them.

Squeak is not just a hustler; she’s a survivor with secrets.

Ronnie is involved in a money-making scheme with his brother Ray (Zachary Grant), who is living in a remote cabin close to the Canadian border. If Ronnie is paranoid, Ray is the king of suspicion. He chastises Ronnie for involving Squeak and Ingrid in his plans.

“These chicks will mess with your mind,” Ray says. “They get this tag team thing going on ‘til you want to wring a neck. They’re sneaky.”

And mess up the plans they do, when Squeak and Ingrid shock everyone in the theater with the surprise ending.

Can’t Run Can’t Dance is creative theater at its best. Strong female characters will leave the audience in stitches. Go see this humorous crime comedy, running through October 5th.

Can’t Run Can’t Dance written by Gregg Henry. Starring John Stout Adams, Juliet Brett, Zachary Grant, and Tracie Lockwood. Directed by Lisa James. The show is presented by New Jersey Repertory Company in Long Branch, New Jersey.

THROUGH OCTOBER 5.  Tickets HERE.

content.rendered:
By Holli Harms

Teenage angst, teenage pain, suicide, parental abuse, abuse by ignoring, unavailability, being lost in your own depression and pain, abuse both physically and verbally.

Blood Orange is a play about pain.

How do teenagers live each day in the in-between? In between adulthood and childhood, their bodies are changing both internally and externally, their desires are both those of the child who needs a safe place and loving arms around them with understanding ears to listen to them, conflicting with the need to be totally independent and autonomous. HOW do they navigate all of this??!

Photo by Gabriela Amerth

Faye (Luisa Galatti) and her friends, Eden (Ana Moioli) and Georgia (Maria Müller), find comfort in each other. But even that is wrought with the same struggles. To exorcise these feelings, Faye turns to religion. A religion she makes up, and it seems to be the only way forward in her truth. It is made up to fit with a desperate hope of answers to questions that have no answers. We believe in monsters and magic when we are small children, but when we have no adult guiding us into adulthood, we can find that we have not grown out of those childhood stories of other worlds and beings. We believe with our minds that we can conjure all of that. Children living in abusive homes will pray to anything to help them.

Blood Orange, written by Abigail Duclos, takes a deep dive into what the loss of family and love can do to a young girl.

The story is a fast tumble into chaos, into anger, torment, and torture. The actors dive just as deep. They are a superb ensemble. They embody the delicate innocence of their in-between world and the deep struggles that grief brings. Grief, we can get lost in its anguish.

And that is where our need to believe in something outside our concrete, defined visible world comes in. And our need for community.

Faye’s father is dead, and her mother, Mariah (Doreen Oliver), is upstairs in her bedroom, locked in her depression. Faye is in high school and is doing all she can to get herself to school, home, fed, and living. No one is there to help her through her PTSD brought on by her father’s choice to end his life. No one but her friend Eden, whose father is emotionally abusing her, and who is easily swayed due to her own feelings of being lost and powerless, and will believe anything to get away from her feelings.

Blood Orange, wonderfully directed by Vernice Miller, is a 90-minute jump-in-the-deep-end journey through the ways in which we push ourselves to cope with desperation and agony to find love and joy.

The cast features: Luísa Galatti as Faye, Ana Moioli as Eden, Maria Müller as Georgia (performing September 11, 13, 19, 21, 22, 27); Luísa Galatti as Faye, Ana Moioli as Eden, Giorgia Valenti as Georgia (performing on September 13 matinee, and September 14, 18, 20 matinee, and September 26, September 27 matinee); and Maria Müller as Faye, Ana Moioli as Eden, Giorgia Valenti as Georgia (performing on September 12, 15, 20, and 25)

Production directed by Vernice Miller with Amelia Estrada as associate director/choreographer; Scenic and Property Design by Ningning Yang; Costumes Designed by Whitney Fabre; and Lighting Designed by Hayley Garcia Parnell

Et Alia Theater: Production and Box Office Management by Covi Loveridge Brannan; Isabel Criado, stage manager

Running Time: 90 minutes with no intermission.

Tickets HERE

A.R.T. New York Theaters 502 W 53rd St, New York, NY 10019

content.rendered:
By Victoria L. Dammer

Sexting has consequences. But sexting your boss instead of your girlfriend? That’s a whole other matter when you involve middle-aged men trying to retrieve the cell phone of the wrong recipient. Caper is an evening of nonsense, chaos, and absurdity in a one-night escapade in New York City.

Phil (Ron Palais) has made a big mistake. Instead of sexting his girlfriend’s telephone number, he sent the sext to his boss, Janet (Anne Klaus). In his moment of life-or-death crisis, he involves his misfit group of friends to recover the phone.

Larry (Richard Cooper), Duke (Asa James), Chris (Christopher Tramantana), Silvia (Celester Rich), and Billy (Sam Gilroy) have toxic, misogynistic views of women. The group of men haven’t developed past their wild man-child youths, and the audience immediately started hysterical laughter at the movie’s opening. The humor — it’s Monty Python attending their poker game when they attempt to devise a solution to Phil’s dilemma. We observed the group’s lack of wisdom, instability, and immature behavior as they comforted Phil. Their inability to handle life makes the movie that much better.

In search of correcting Phil’s perverse midlife crisis mistake, the group lands in a sex club, dressing up in a variety of costumes that add to the harebrained adventure. Regardless of the symbolism, it made all attendees laugh. The night evolves scene after scene, each funnier than the last. What really shines in this movie is the lesson that genuine friendship survives when you need your posse the most.

And at the finish of the evening, not to spoil the ending, the group of men receive insight into the female sex they don’t understand or never will.

Dean Imperial wrote and directed this movie. Caper has a group of actors that work so well together that one gets the impression they are not acting at all. This movie was so insanely and innocently funny that you need to see it several times.

Caper, written and directed by Dean Imperial. Starring Richard Cooper, Asa James, Anne Klaus, Christopher Tramantana, Michael Panes, Sam Gilroy, and Celester Rich, at LOOK Cinemas W. 57th.

Running time is 88 minutes.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

For the first time in the four-and-a-half years of development, the new folk musical Colorado Silver, by Emma Harlow and Ciera Miller, and directed by Miller, was shared on a stage. It’s score, written entirely by Harlow, completely shook the jam-packed room at 54 Below. Harlow & Miller, 2023 Jonathan Larson Grant Honorable Mentions, showcased their long-awaited score along with a notable cast. Familiar faces from past and upcoming national tours and Broadway stages alike left me with only space for wanting to see this entire musical from the overture to final bows on a stage large enough to hold this energy and crowd—a Broadway stage.

As soon as the music started, I felt something powerful— I felt I had a sneak peak, a front row seat at something larger.

With a show in development, I did not know what to expect, and I was immediately intrigued. Straightaway, Cole Vaughan left me leaning over the table, in awe, astonishment, and disbelief for how this cast and their presence felt like dynamite had been lit to fuel this concert. The story line itself initially reminded me of a story prompt for young mystery or horror writers: two friends get lost in the woods; but this story suddenly swerved into darker–and simultaneously a more fragile–territory.

“There’s something about these woods…you’re never alone.”

It’s the 1800’s and two sisters, Audrey (Emma Harlow) and Liza (Bridgette Kinsella) are making their way west when they encounter an abandoned mining town–“Way out west between the cold rocky mountains…”

We’re told of the stories of the Lady in Blue, the darkness and vastness of the woods. “…Can you hear the blue woman cryin? Nobody knows her name; now her face is torn away…can you bear to see the sight, somethings are better not remembered!”

We wonder if these sisters will stick together, if the night will consume them. When one sister wants out and the other wants to continue, will they come together? Will they even make it out alive?

“What’s the use of living for the words of the dead? What’s the use of loving if you can’t forgive?”

When the first song finished (and at the conclusion of every single song thereafter), my date started whooping as though his favorite team had just scored a game winning point (mind you, he is NOT a musical theater guy, nor is he a loud individual). His response both surprised and delighted me, and I realized that that shiver that ran up my torso was a feeling felt throughout the entire room.

Colorado Silver is a show about forgiveness, sacrifice, redemption, and hope.

“When it’s cold outside, and summer blows away, where will you hide?”

I will confidently predict that Colorado Silver is something and it will be somewhere, somewhere soon. With an upcoming industry performance in a few months, I have hope in Miller & Harlow’s new musical.

One of my first thoughts was, This is going to be at Longacre (and not even because Swept Away’s Hunter Brown had joined the stage as “Buckskin Joe”). I both regretted thinking it because of the theater’s track record with shows closing far too soon—(if you know, you know)—but also Colorado Silver IS the space’s vibe and easily falls into the folk-music, uniquely tragic, and that singular favorite character succumbing to death, like past productions at Longacre.

Whether you’ve already caught wind (or that distinct shiver through your body) of this up and coming eerily striking piece or have yet to experience its folksy brilliance, Colorado Silver is a ghost story that won’t stay dead.

Produced by Jonathan Larson Grant Honorable Mentions Miller & Harlow, music and lyrics by Emma Harlow, directed by Ciera Miller, and featuring special guest vocalists.

FEATURING: Hunter Brown (Swept Away) as Buckskin Joe; Katelyn Crall (Hadestown national tour) as Gemma; Jaylon Crump (Jesus Christ Superstar national tour, Rent national tour, Hadestown national tour) as Pastor Dyer; Emma Harlow as Audrey; Janaysia Gethers as Flossy; Bridgette Kinsella as Liza; Megan Masako; Haley (Mean Girls national tour, Wicked national tour) as Silver Heels; Erin McMillen (Hadestown national tour) as Talullah; Chris Ruetten as Hal; Kate Short as Loretta; Joseph Thor as Horace; Cole Vaughan (Floyd Collins) as Yammerin.

Jessie Bittner, fiddle; Elias Neuman-Donihue, guitar; Jessie Ong, percussion; and Leo Weisskoff, upright bass.

Colorado Silver by Miller & Harlow was in concert at 54 Below, 254 W 54th St. Cellar, NYC 10019, on Sept. 6, 2025. Tickets for upcoming 54 Below shows can be purchased here or by calling (646) 476-3551.

title.rendered: Patient 13 Written and Performed by Gail Thomas

content.rendered:
by Betsyann Faiella

Patient 13, the true story of Gail Thomas’s cancer and life trip of about a dozen years ago is written and delivered with immense skill. The humor, wisdom and candor abound. The intimate space of Pangea in the East Village was an unusual setting; there was no pianist, no singing. Just a really smart, funny, single, independent woman, seamlessly, hilariously, sincerely recounting her relationship with a reluctant romantic partner, her cancer diagnosis and treatment (after much Google research), and her insights and lessons learned. At two years cancer free, she was invited to participate in a study using Psylocibin to lift depression. After admitting that she just might be depressed, Thomas became Patient 13 in a group of 29 people in a groundbreaking study originating at UCLA and Johns Hopkins.

Her monologue is a reminder that we’re in charge of our own destinies (to a point). It also reminded me of friends’ cancer trips: how one can count on people being assholes, as well as others being angels – and sometimes they’re both. Her sort-of boyfriend, Wes, was sort-of reliable for chores and sex. Family asked what they could do, but when she asked her mother to sweep her room, mother demurred. Her sister declined to do research, but sent money for a cleaning lady. One couple did wash her shower curtain.

When she was told by her original surgeon (after surgery) that he was wrong about her diagnosis and she might very well die without an extreme course of radiation and chemotherapy, Thomas spent hours researching her disease and meeting with other doctors until she found one she trusted enough. As it turns out, she picked a winner and recovered. There was one more giant glitch during her recovery, and it was so insane that it succeeded in putting an end to her relationship with Wes.

Her delivery of this funny, touching work was without one hiccup. While a performance outside of NYC might be met with shock and awe and giggles and guffaws, we New Yorkers (in an audience predominantly made of women- what’s that about??) did a lot of grateful nodding at the descriptions of dating Wes, who seemed good for semi-reliability, sex and home repairs; her googling how to do EVERTHING; the search for a doctor who cared to find the right treatment for the patient; dating as a bald woman during chemo; admitting to depression and taking a chance on something wild and out of character (as Thomas was not experienced with drugs when asked if she would like to participate in the Psylocibin study). I also suspect there were many cancer survivors in the audience.  It was more of an internal experience than laugh out loud, but not without tons of humor.

The Psylocibin trip was recounted in detail. It left Thomas with a sense of the interconnectedness of everyone and more faith in herself as an artist and a resolve to be less safe with her choices. She was forced to re-examine relationships and her own decisions.

“I get rid of all the toxic people. And there is no one left,” says Thomas.

I was in awe of Thomas’s ability to deliver the script: the excellent writing, the performing of it, the timing. There was no waiting on laughs. It’s just not that type of performance, though it’s extremely funny and shocking too. We were all nodding at the parts of ourselves we recognized in Thomas, and the gratitude for this gift of her story burst forth from the crowd when she uttered her final words.

Patient 13 will play at Pangea again on Sept 18 and Sept 20 2025 at 7PM. Pangea is in Manhattan at 178 Second Ave. between 11th and 12th Streets. Phone: 212-995-0900. Dinner and drinks are available.

content.rendered:
By Brittany Crowell

Alexander McQueen, fashion designer and storyteller, was known for pushing boundaries and for the uncommon and sometimes uncouth theatrical presentation of his work and designs.  At many points in his career, he pushed back against the fashion industry’s tendency to turn designers into hand-bag-makers and to appease commercial lines and chains.

It feels quite out of place, therefore, that to get to the House of McQueen, one must enter through a gift shop of somewhat gaudy and tacky items for sale; bearing the McQueen name, and yet none of his aesthetic or design.  These items, devoid of design and storytelling, are so outside of the ethos of the artist.

Spencer R Petro in costume by Kaye Voyce; photo by Thomas Hodges.

The play itself, produced Off-Broadway at The Mansion, similarly missteps.  The grey platform stage highlights the colorful costumes and recreations of McQueens designs (expertly brought to life by costume designer Kaye Voyce), however these designs are shadowed by a looming, overhanging LED. The LED ceiling and its counterpart LED backdrop aim to set the scenes through amorphous imagery that lacks specificity and impact. The tech-heavy design, while in line with the technical innovations lauded by McQueen in his fashion shows, doesn’t push the boundary to feel up to snuff with the work or legacy of McQueen himself.

Following the story of McQueen’s life from childhood through his early death at 41, the play features a strong ensemble of actors who bring lots of energy to the piece.  Luke Newton, as Lee Alexander McQueen, gives a heartfelt performance of the troubled artist whose gruff charm both baffles and wins the hearts of the audience.  Catherine LeFrere also shines as the enigmatic socialite and fashion editor Izzy Blow, who jump-starts McQueen’s career and follows him throughout.

A highlight of the evening is a small exhibit just to the side of the theater where they have featured an array of McQueen memorabilia, showcasing some of the dresses that get discussed in length within the piece itself.  As someone who doesn’t follow the fashion world extensively, I enjoyed seeing how the artist’s personal story impacted his work and learning more about his humble beginnings and exciting career.

Part of what the play itself taught me was how McQueen actively fought against commercialization and fitting within a box.  As an artist, he was always shocking, pushing boundaries, and exploring new methods. It was disappointing to me, therefore, that this theatrical “requiem to McQueen” was so …. quiet; leaned so heavily into the commercial nature of theater; followed a somewhat standard narrative formula without pushing any boundaries.  And at the end of the piece, the audience was asked to then exit through the gift shop.  I think McQueen (similarly to Banksy who so famously coined the phrase) would frown on this and task us to dig deeper, be braver, go further.

 

HOUSE OF MCQUEEN – written by Darrah Cloud

Directed by Sam Helfrich

FEATURING: Luke Newton; Emily Skinner, Cody Braverman, Tim Creavin, Fady Demian, Matthew Evy, Joe Joseph, Denis Lambert, Margaret, Odetter, Spencer, R. Petro, Jonina Thorsteinsdottir, Sam Dash, James Evenas, Krystal Riggs, Jackie Sanders, Chris Thorn, and Catherine LeFrere

Scenic design, Jason Ardizzone-West; costume design, Kaye Voyce; lighting design, Robert Wierzel; video and projection design, Brad Peterson; original music, Andres Martin; sound design, G Clausen; hair, wig, & makeup design, Tommy Kurzman; props supervisor, Oscar Escobedo; choreographer, Benjamin Freedman; dialect coach, Deborah Hecht; intimacy coordinator, NJ Agwuna.  Executive producer, Rick Lazes; creative director, Gary James McQueen; based on the book by Rick Lazes and Seth Koch. The Mansiona t Hudson Yards (508 W 37th St, New York, NY 10018); through October 19.  https://www.thehouseofmcqueen.com/

content.rendered:
TM – not yet

I was once told that all Russian stories are written in a minor key. “I am profoundly unhappy,” pretty much sums up each character in The Mutt, now playing at IATI Theater through September 21.

I don’t know if you know Dostoevsky’s book The Brothers Karamazov or not (if not, it should at least be on your “Someday I’m going to read this” list). A small part of the 750-page novel deals with a dog named Zhuchka. Only a small part, deep in the book, but of the many many themes in this book, this small part re-emphasizes prominent motifs of identity, redemption, death, and rebirth that course through this literary masterpiece.

Fourteen-year-old Ilyusha, feeling pressured by his peers to show off, throws a piece of bread with a pin in it to the stray dog Zhuchika, who eats it, howls and runs off, appearing obviously in pain. Ilyusha, horrified that he has killed the dog, laments his despicable action.

Ilyusha becomes sick and lies in bed dying, still feeling guilty about what he did to the dog. One of his gang, Kolya, arrives with Zhuchka. The dog had survived and evidently never swallowed the pin. After finding him, Kolya even trained him to perform tricks, and when he brings Zhuchka to Ilyusha’s bedside, the boy is overjoyed, as it has brought him some solace to the death he is anticipating.

This intimate production takes this small story and dives deep into its themes through staging, choreography, film, and music. What you’ll get is layers of meaning, identity created from the outside in, an unapologetic presentation of the struggle of life to find its way in a bleak land, expressed through a number of different media.

The set is an interior barn-like structure that is utilized like playground equipment. Course, functional, and appropriate to the play and its story.

There are beautifully filmed backdrops projected throughout the play of a frozen, heavily snow-covered black and white landscape, with a dog expectantly looking at the camera, bringing the only life and hope to the frigidness.

The Mutt is a step away from traditional linear storytelling, delivering nuanced pictures of strained relationships, internally as well as with others, and the struggle to find where one’s true self resides.

If you’re a lover of Dostoevsky, it’s a must-see, as this appreciation and love of his work is not often dramatized.

—–

Streetcar Productions and Art Against Humanity present the world premiere of The Mutt
Adapted by Anoushka Nesterova from Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov
September 10–21, 2025 | IATI Theater | New York City

Directed by Anoushka Nesterova and Elena Che.

Cast: Fabio Bernardis, Jaden Cavalleri, Tommy Dougherty, Benjamin Nowak, Marcus Troy, Sasha Litovchenko, Alina Mhailevschi, and Anoushka Nesterova.

Choreography by Gisela Quinteros, Composer Evgeniy Grebnev, Set Designer Alyona Sotnikova, Cinematographer Anastasia Slepchenkova, and Lighting Designer Lev Chesnov.

Running time 1 hour 40 minutes

Tickets: https://tinyurl.com/the-mutt
Website: https://themuttplay.com/

content.rendered:
By Eryn Malafronte

If you are anything like me, or most people, addiction may have touched a part of your life over the years ; for me it was caffeine, sugar, and yes even alcohol, especially being an actress who moved to the city at 18. That being said, I did not come into this with the expectation of a show shouldering this subject matter would/should be considered a dark comedy. I find the balance of a dark comedy very tricky, the “dark” scenes hold the gravitas which makes the audience appreciate and even long for the levity of a comedic song. I love the feeling of laughing through tears, so while I wasn’t expecting a dark comedy for a show about AA, it makes sense. Progress isn’t linear or one note, and neither is recovery. Like the show itself advertises, It’s messy, it’s imperfect, it’s REAL, my only wish was it would show more of the latter two.

 

SOBER SONGS is a dark comedy that centers around six young adults in recovery at a local AA. While I think the singing in this show is beautiful , and the value professional, when aspects of a show are so polished, the caveat is that it makes the missteps so blatant. And while it’s still certainly a show to see during its run, I would be lying if I did not say I was left wanting more out of particular characters and plot lines of this show. 

 

One thing I will briefly touch upon, because it is so small, but if someone plays a guitar in the show, knowing how to play what the audience is hearing may seem like such a tiny detail, but when coupled with an amazing set and, and clearly a talented production team, those little minute details tend to stick out, especially when the guitar isn’t really necessary to the scene or even the character.The cast itself was smaller with nine people, three members of which really don’t get any text in the show , except for maybe one or two lines during the group numbers, specifically the opener of the show “I’m an alcoholic” I hold no issue with small casts, however when so many characters are utilized so often, It makes me wish I had more context of the three underutilized performers I see on stage, in all the group numbers, that don’t get to share more of their story.

 

Another area that I was left wanting more was in the way the women in this show were portrayed. There were three female leads, Angie (Melani Carrié), Bri ( Merrill Mitchell), and Nina (Jocelyn Darci Trimmer), all of these women were phenomenal in their own way, but almost all of their text in the show centered around a male counterpart or love interest. These women were so talented, I wish I could have seen more of their struggles in a way that wasn’t told through their love interest plot line. Each musical number was separated by a short scene, but the short scenes held the bulk of the serious dialogue that moved the play along, which I felt were cut too short. One character in the show I felt suffered from this was Cap ( Bernard Holcomb) who played the head sponsor that led the bulk of the meetings. Holcomb is one seriously talented performer whose character plays a fulcrum of sorts in the lives of these young adults by keeping them balanced and offering advice and wisdom. Cap was delivering his personal story later on in the show on how he entered the program, it was a very short scene, but it was my favorite scene in the show, and it’s THAT writing I wish was scattered more throughout the runtime, it felt more like an overall comedy, when so many comedic songs are in between and there is  no time to let the serious scenes breathe, or let the audience recover.

Lastly, I wish more context was given towards all of these characters, and that the personal relationships of every character were more established, particularly with the characters Roque (Jason Fio) and Dean (Henry Ryeder ), for the audience to care more about the obstacle that comes later on in act one. I would have loved to see the struggles and perspective of more POC in the show going through the program, as opposed to briefly touching upon them and focusing more on the story line of a straight white male. 

 

All of this being said, this show has an incredibly talented cast, The comedy portion of this show was apparent, and we very much enjoyed ourselves, seeing as how we watched opening night, It can only improve from here.

If you have 12 steps to take, one of them should be into Theater Row to see SOBER SONGS.

 

SOBER SONGS playing at Theater Row in  Theatre 3 (410 West 42nd Street, NY NY 10036)

 

 Now through Sunday, September 28th. Tickets are $39-$89 and are available at bfany.org/theatre-row

 

MICHAEL LEVIN (Book, Music & Lyrics), CHRIS MACKIN (Director), MEGAN ROE (Choreographer), BRIAN REYNOLDS (Music Director), Photos by Shawn Salley

STARRING: Melanie Carrié, Jason Fio, Bernard Holcomb, Merrill Mitchell, Henry Ryeder, Jocelyn Darci Trimmer, Lennie Disanto, Jake Kleve, Sarah Sun Park.

title.rendered: BOOK REVIEW: Lin-Manuel Miranda: The Education of an Artist

content.rendered:
By Nicole Itkin

Lin-Manuel Miranda is a prolific writer whose work has deeply impacted the world of theater and film. So, I was thrilled to review the new biography Lin-Manuel Miranda: The Education of an Artist by Daniel Pollack-Pelzner. And it did not disappoint. 

Through an extensive collection of interviews, Lin-Manuel Miranda: The Education of an Artist walks us through the stories of Miranda’s projects. From Hamilton to Encanto, Pollack-Pelzner pulls us in, making us feel like we’re part of the production stories, waiting with bated breath even when we’ve already seen the finished products—and their success. 

Pollack-Pelzner shows how closely and carefully Miranda worked through key problems. “Who was Aaron Burr? What did he want? Cracking Hamilton’s psychology proved far easier than fathoming the man who shot him. Lin-Manuel instinctively understood Hamilton’s immigrant ambition, his relentless energy, his drive to write as if he was running out of time. But what motivated Burr?” (p. 215) Pollack-Pelzner goes on to explain how Miranda came to understand Burr’s character, and it is striking to see just how thought-out and thought through Miranda’s reasoning is. There is such joy on the page when the pieces connect and it all comes together. It is logically fascinating and artistically stunning. 

The book discusses Miranda’s fear upon first seeing Tick Tick…Boom. “Larson was singing on the eve of his thirtieth birthday, having spent the past decade working on a sci-fi rock musical that no one would produce. He heard the clock of mortality tick-ticking away while his friends left the city or moved into higher-paying fields…[Miranda had] thought he was going to follow Larson to musical-theater stardom. Was he more likely to follow him to failure? Would he have the courage to keep creating even if he never lived to see professional success?” (p. 83) There’s so many questions here: What is the value of creation without success? What do we do when we find out our role models were racked with  uncertainty? The questions, the fear….they hit on something deeply felt and wonderfully rich. 

But the text doesn’t just leave us with questions; it tries to answer them. “[His mother, Luz] helped him breathe deeply, sang to him, and reminded him that every experience, however painful, was transitory: ‘This too shall pass.’ And she told him that even a stressful episode might prove useful. ‘You want to be a writer? Remember this feeling. It’s all grist for the mill.'” (p. 45) All of it can mean something: All the pain, all the joy. This book is about Miranda doing just that—taking pain, taking joy, taking a character, and making art out of it. 

This is a fantastic read for the writer, the actor, or the simply curious. It is replete with joy and hard work. In peering into Miranda’s life, there are a million possible detours that the book could take. However, Pollack-Pelzner walks the fine line of being extraordinarily detailed while remaining focused on the stories he is telling. Not only does the book take us through Miranda’s incredible life, it also takes us into his thinking and his decisions; it’s educational, inspiring, and downright fun to read. 

 

Lin-Manuel Miranda: The Education of an Artist by Daniel Pollack-Pelzner 

Publish date: September 9, 2025

Link to purchase here: https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Lin-Manuel-Miranda/Daniel-Pollack-Pelzner/9781668014707
